en: I bow to that Supreme Self, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, by whose play of ignorance the creations of the elements and their derivatives arise.
I bow to that supreme teacher, the lord of ascetics named Nṛsiṃha, by whose disciple-lions the elephants of dualism were driven away. 2.
I bow to the venerable Veṅkaṭanātha, the inhabitants of Velāṅguḍi, the teachers of the world, who are the originators of all philosophical systems. (3)
By whom the commentary named Tarkacūḍāmaṇi was composed upon the Cintāmaṇi, delighting the wise and elucidating the ten commentaries. ||4||
Therefore, for the sake of the enlightenment of those who are dull-witted, this *Paribhāṣā*, which relies upon the meaning of the Vedānta,
is composed by Dharmarāja Ādhvarīndra.

Indeed, among the four aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—it is liberation alone that is the supreme aim, because its permanence is established by such scriptural passages as, "He does not return again. As for the other three, their impermanence is understood both through direct perception and through scriptural passages such as, "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes. And since that liberation arises from the knowledge of Brahman, Brahman, the knowledge thereof, and its means of proof are now investigated in detail.

In this context, *pramāṇa* is the instrument of valid cognition (*pramā*). Here, the nature of validity (*pramātva*) as distinguished from memory (*smṛti*) consists in being a cognition whose object is an unapprehended and unsublated thing; whereas the nature of validity common to memory consists in being a cognition whose object is an unsublated thing. Since it is accepted that even formless time is perceptible by the senses, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*), because each such cognition has as its object a particular moment not previously apprehended by the preceding cognition.

Furthermore, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), in the case of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*), there is no difference between the cognitions; rather, as long as the jar manifests, there is only one single modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of the jar, and not many, because it is admitted that a mental modification persists until the arising of another modification that is opposed to it. Consequently, the cognition of the jar and so forth, which consists of the consciousness reflected therein, is also only one for that duration; thus, there is not even the slightest suspicion of the definition being too narrow (*avyāpti*). Now, an objection may be raised: since the jar and such objects are false and sublated according to our doctrine, how can the cognition thereof be considered valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?

It is said: For the sublation (*bādha*) of jars and the like occurs only after the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman, according to the Śruti: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? However, there is no sublation during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), according to the Śruti: "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another. Thus, by the term "unsublated" (*abādhita*), what is intended is non-sublation during the state of transmigratory existence; therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the valid cognition of jars and the like. As it has been said: "Just as the notion of the body being the self is accepted as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),"
"In the same way, this worldly [knowledge] is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) until the ascertainment of the Self.
This means "until the ascertainment of the Self," that is, up to the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of Brahman. "Worldly" refers to the cognition of jars and so forth.

Those means of valid cognition are sixfold, distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), comparison (upamāna), verbal testimony (śabda), presumption (arthāpatti), and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi).
In this context, the instrument (karaṇa) of direct valid cognition (pratyakṣapramā) is the means of direct perception (pratyakṣapramāṇa).

Direct valid cognition here is consciousness (caitanya) itself, according to the Vedic scripture: "That which is immediate and direct" (*yatsākṣādaparokṣāt*). The term *aparokṣāt* has the meaning of "direct" (*aparokṣam*).

[Objection: But since consciousness (*caitanya*) is beginningless, how can the eyes and other [senses] possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by being its instruments? [Response: It is said: although consciousness is beginningless, the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that manifests it is produced through the contact of the senses and so forth; thus, consciousness qualified by such a modification is said to be "beginning-endowed" (*ādimat*). Furthermore, because the modification serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for knowledge, the term "knowledge" is used metaphorically (*upacāra*) with respect to the modification. As it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Because the term 'knowledge' is used metaphorically with respect to the modification of the internal organ."

Now, one might ask: how can there be a modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of transformation for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is partless? It is as follows: first of all, the internal organ is not partless, because, being a substance that has a beginning, it must possess parts. Its having a beginning is established by such scriptural texts as, "It created the mind" (*tan mano 'sṛjata*). Furthermore, the fact that knowledge in the form of a modification is an attribute of the mind is evidenced by the scripture: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are indeed the mind. Here, the word "intelligence" (*dhī*) denotes knowledge in the form of a modification. For this very reason, desire and the rest are also attributes of the mind.

Objection: If desire and the like are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), how can the experience "I desire," "I fear," and so forth—which apprehends them as being the attributes of the Self—be justified? Reply: It is said: Just as there is the common usage "the iron ball burns" even though the iron ball lacks the power to burn, because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the fire which is the locus of that burning power; so too, due to the superimposition of identity with the internal organ which undergoes transformation into the forms of pleasure and so forth, the usage "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so on arises.

[Objection: But since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is a sense-organ (*indriya*), how can it be an object of perception, given that sense-organs are themselves beyond the senses? [Reply: There is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that the internal organ is a sense-organ. If you argue that the statement in the *Bhagavadgītā*, "The senses are six, with the mind as the sixth," serves as proof—no, for there is no rule that the completion of a numerical count of sense-organs must be achieved by a sense-organ alone. This is seen in the case of the injunction, "The priests eat the *iḍā* oblation with the sacrificer as the fifth," where the number five belonging to the priests is completed by the sacrificer, even though he is not a priest.

This is because, in passages such as "He taught the Vedas, with the Mahābhārata as the fifth," we see that the number five belonging to the Vedas is completed by including the Bhārata, which is not a Veda; and furthermore, because scriptures such as "The objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the objects" indicate that the mind is not an organ (indriya).

Nor should it be argued that if the mind were not a sense organ (*anindriya*), the directness (*sākṣātkāratva*) of the perception of pleasure and so forth would not exist because it would not be produced by a sense organ. For directness does not belong to a cognition simply by virtue of being produced by a sense organ; otherwise, inference and other forms of knowledge would also result in being direct, since they too are produced by the mind. Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the Lord’s cognition—which is not produced by a sense organ—would lack directness. If one asks what constitutes the determinant of perceptuality in the established system (*siddhānta*): do you ask for the determinant of perceptuality as it pertains to the cognition itself, or as it pertains to the object?

Regarding the first [type of knowledge], we say that there is non-difference between the consciousness delimited by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacaitanya*) and the consciousness delimited by the object (*viṣayāvacchinnacaitanya*). To explain: consciousness is threefold—consciousness as the object (*viṣayacaitanya*), consciousness as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacaitanya*), and consciousness as the knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*). Among these, consciousness delimited by a jar or the like is consciousness as the object; consciousness delimited by a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) is consciousness as the means of valid cognition; and consciousness delimited by the internal organ is consciousness as the knower.

In this regard, just as the water of a pond, having emerged through a hole and entered a field via the medium of a canal, assumes the very same shape as that field—such as being quadrangular and so forth—so too the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is of the nature of fire, emerges through the doors of the eyes and other senses, reaches the location of objects such as a jar, and transforms into the form of those objects, such as a jar; that very transformation is called a "mental mode" (*vṛtti*). However, in cases such as inference, there is no physical movement of the internal organ to the location of the fire and so forth, because the fire and such are not in sensory contact with the eyes and other organs.

And so, in cases of perception such as "this is a jar," because the jar and its corresponding mental modification (*vṛtti*) are both present together in one and the same location externally, the consciousness delimited by both is indeed one and the same; for even though there are two delimiters—the mental modification and the object such as the jar—they do not produce a division [of consciousness] since they occupy the same space. For this very reason, the space delimited by a jar situated inside a hut does not differ from the space delimited by the hut itself.

Likewise, in the case of the perceptual instance "this jar," because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the jar is in contact with the jar, the consciousness delimited by the jar and the consciousness delimited by that modification are non-different; thus, the cognition of the jar is perceptual with respect to its aspect as the form of the jar. Furthermore, since the consciousness delimited by pleasure, pain, and so forth, and the consciousness delimited by the corresponding modification, are invariably delimited by two adjuncts (*upādhi*) situated in the same location, the cognition "I am happy" or "I am miserable" is necessarily perceptual.

If it is objected that, in this way, even the recollection of one's own past pleasure and so forth would result in being a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to the portion consisting of that pleasure and so forth, we say: no. In that case, because the pleasure being recollected is past while the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of memory is present, the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) belong to different times. Consequently, there is a difference between the consciousnesses delimited by them (*tattadavacchinnacaitanya*). This is because, provided they occupy the same location, it is precisely their simultaneity that serves as the cause for the non-difference of the entities delimited by them (*upadheya*).

If, however, the mere fact of being located in the same place were the cause for the non-difference of the substrate (upadheya), then, in order to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti) to such memories as "I was happy before," the qualification of "presentness" must be applied to the object.

[Objection: But if this is so, when one's own merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are present, are known through verbal testimony and the like, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such verbal cognitions and the like; for in that case, the consciousness delimited by merit and the like and the consciousness delimited by its [corresponding] mental mode (*vṛtti*) are one and the same. [Reply: No, because "fitness" (*yogyatva*) is also a qualifier of the object. Although there is no difference in their both being attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), nature alone—determined by the force of the results (*phala*)—is the resort for explaining why some things are fit and others are unfit.

Otherwise, even in the Nyāya system, since there is no difference in their being attributes of the self (*ātmadharma*), it would be difficult to avoid the consequence that dharma and so forth would be perceptible, just like pleasure and the like. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the cognition produced by a sentence such as "you are happy" during the state of the actual existence of pleasure would have to be perceptual; for this is indeed accepted, since in cases such as "you are the tenth," the admission of immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge even from a word is accepted when the object is in close proximity.

For this very reason, even a cognition such as "the mountain possesses fire" is indirect (*parokṣa*) with respect to the aspect of fire, but direct (*aparokṣa*) with respect to the aspect of the mountain. This is because there is no mutual difference between the consciousness delimited by the mountain and so forth, and the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) that has issued forth externally. However, with respect to the aspect of fire, since there is no outward extension of the mental modification, there is a mutual difference between the consciousness delimited by fire and the consciousness that constitutes the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇacaitanya*).

And thus there is the experience: "I see the mountain; I infer fire. Furthermore, according to the Nyāya school, there would be the undesirable consequence of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form, "I infer the mountain. However, in an inference where the subject (*pakṣa*) is not in contact with the senses, the cognition is indirect (*parokṣa*) in all its aspects. Even in a cognition such as "the sandalwood is fragrant," the aspect of the sandalwood block is direct (*aparokṣa*), while the aspect of fragrance is indirect; for fragrance is not suitable for the visual sense-organ, and thus the aforementioned definition—consisting of suitability—is absent in that respect.

Nor should it be argued that if both mediacy (*parokṣatva*) and immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) were admitted in a single cognition, their status as universals (*jāti*) would be lost; for this is precisely what we accept. This is because the technical distinction between being a universal and being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) lacks any basis in valid cognition, as it falls outside the scope of all means of knowledge. Indeed, perception such as "this is a jar" is the proof for the existence of *jar-ness* (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, but not for its status as a universal. Since the probandum in the form of "universality" itself is unestablished, there is no room for an inference to prove it either.

Furthermore, because the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished and because the entire phenomenal world is distinct from Brahman and impermanent, the status of being a universal (*jāti*), which is defined by eternality and inherence, is unestablished in respect to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like. In this very same way, the status of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhitva*) is to be refuted. In such cases as "the mountain possesses fire," there is no contradiction whatsoever in the occurrence of both mediacy (*parokṣatva*) and immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) within a single consciousness, provided one accepts a distinction between the mental modifications (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) regarding the aspect of the mountain and the aspect of the fire, based on the difference in the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of those respective modifications.

And thus, in the first case, the perceptuality of a cognition delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of a particular form consists in its non-difference from the consciousness delimited by the present object suitable for that respective sense organ;
in the second case, however, the perceptuality of an object such as a jar consists in its non-difference from the knower (*pramātṛ*).

If it be objected: "How can there be non-difference between a jar or the like and the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), given the contradiction with the experience of difference in the form 'I see this'?"—it is replied: Non-difference from the knower does not mean identity; rather, it is the absence of any existence apart from the existence of the knower. Thus, because a jar or the like is superimposed upon the consciousness delimited by itself, the existence of the jar is nothing other than the existence of the object-consciousness (*viṣaya-caitanya*), for we do not admit the existence of a superimposed object to be distinct from the existence of its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

And since object-consciousness, according to the manner previously described, is indeed the subject-consciousness (*pramātṛcaitanya*), it is established that the existence of the jar and so forth is nothing other than the existence of the subject, because the subject-consciousness alone is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the jar and so on; thus, the perceptuality of the jar and so forth is proven.

In cases such as inference, however, because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) does not go to the location of the fire and so forth, the consciousness delimited by the fire is not identical with the subject-consciousness; therefore, the existence of the fire and so forth is distinct from the existence of the subject, and thus there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

If it is argued that even so, in cases such as an inference whose object is merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that merit and demerit are perceptible—since the consciousness delimited by merit and so forth is non-different from the consciousness of the knower, and thus the existence of merit and so forth does not exceed the existence of the knower—the answer is no; for "fitness" (*yogyatva*) is also a qualification of the object.

If it is argued that even so, in the case of the perceptual instance "the pot is colored," there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the size (parimāṇa) and other qualities residing in the pot are also perceived—because the consciousness delimited by color (rūpāvacchinna-caitanya) and the consciousness delimited by size are one and the same, and since the consciousness delimited by size is non-different from the subject-consciousness (pramātṛ-caitanya) when the consciousness delimited by color is non-different from the subject-consciousness, the existence of size and so forth is not distinct from the existence of the subject—[we reply: no, because [perceptibility] also requires being conditioned by a mental modification (vṛtti) bearing that respective form.

Because it is a qualification of the knower (*pramātṛ*): since at the time of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of color, there is an absence of a modification having the form of dimension (*parimāṇa*) and so forth, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as the existence [of the object] is not non-different from the consciousness of the knower as conditioned by a modification having the form of dimension and so forth.

If it is objected: "In that case, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding mental modification (*vṛtti*), because, for fear of infinite regress, one does not admit a further modification as the object of a modification; thus, the aforementioned definition—which consists in being conditioned by a modification having its own form—is absent therein"—we reply: No. Even if, for fear of infinite regress, a modification is not the object of another modification, we nevertheless accept that it is self-objectifying (*svaviṣaya*). Consequently, the condition of "having the same existence as the subject-consciousness conditioned by a modification whose object is itself" is possible even in that case.

Thus, although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its attributes (*dharma*), and so forth are objects of the pure witness (*kevalasākṣin*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the aforementioned definition, because one accepts that they possess mental modifications (*vṛtti*) corresponding to their respective forms. Nor should it be argued that accepting the internal organ, its attributes, and so forth as objects of mental modification contradicts the acceptance that they are known by the pure witness alone; for being an object of the witness alone does not mean being an object of the witness without a mental modification, but rather being an object of the witness without the operation of the senses, inference, or other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For this very reason, the Teachers (Ācāryas) accepted in their commentary on the *Ahaṃkāra* that there is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) having the form of "I" (*ahaṃ*). And for this same reason, the traditional authorities have accepted in the case of illusory silver that there is a modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) having the form of silver. Thus, since the definition consisting of being "qualified by a modification" exists in the case of the internal organ and its attributes—which are cognizable solely by the Witness (*sākṣin*)—there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

Thus, this is the distilled meaning: the perceptibility of an object consists in its being fit [for cognition] while lacking any existence apart from the existence of the cognizer’s consciousness as conditioned by a mental modification (vṛtti) in its own form. In that regard, the various types of contact—such as conjunction, inherence in the conjoined, and so forth—are merely instrumental in producing a mental modification that manifests consciousness. And that modification is fourfold: doubt, certainty, egoity, and recollection. This being the case, although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is one, it is designated as "mind" (*manas*), "intellect" (*buddhi*), "ego" (*ahaṅkāra*), and "thought" (*citta*) according to the specific modification. As it has been said: [The verse follows: *mano buddhirahaṅkāraścittam karaṇam antaram / saṃśayo niścayo garvaḥ smaraṇaṃ viṣayā ime //* (The internal organs are mind, intellect, ego, and thought; these are the objects: doubt, certainty, pride, and recollection.)
The internal instruments are the intellect (manas), the faculty of thought (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the mind (citta).
Doubt, certainty, pride, and recollection—these are their respective objects. 1.
And that perception is of two kinds, distinguished as conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

Among these, conceptual perception is knowledge that apprehends a relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), such as the knowledge "I know the jar," and so forth. Non-conceptual perception, however, is knowledge that does not apprehend a relation; for example, the knowledge produced by sentences such as "This is that Devadatta" or "That thou art."

If it is argued that this knowledge is verbal and not perception because it is not produced by the sense organs, we say no. For being produced by the sense organs is not the determinant factor for perception, as that has been refuted. Rather, it has been stated that [perception] consists in the non-difference of the consciousness of the means of knowledge and the consciousness of the object, provided that the object is a present one capable of being perceived.

And likewise, because the knowledge produced by the sentence "This is that Devadatta" has a proximate object, it is accepted that there is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) extending outward; thus, through the non-difference between the consciousness delimited by Devadatta and the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛttyavacchinna-caitanya*), the knowledge produced by the sentence "This is that Devadatta" is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*).

The same applies to the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). In that case, since the subject (*pramātṛ*) itself is the object, the non-difference between those two [consciousnesses] exists.

But surely, since the cognition produced by a sentence involves the apprehension of the relation between word-meanings, how can it be non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka)? It is said in reply: in being the object of a sentence-generated cognition, the status of being a relation between word-meanings is not the determining factor; for otherwise, even an unintended relation would result in being an object of that cognition. Rather, the determining factor is the status of being the intended object of the speaker's purport (tātparya).

And in the present context, since the purport of the Vedāntas is determined to be the pure Brahman—beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1) and concluding with "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou, Śvetaketu" (*ibid.* 6.8.7)—how could it cause the cognition of a relation that is not its object? This very thing is the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) of sentences such as "That art thou": namely, their capacity to produce a true knowledge that does not involve a relation. As it has been said:

"That which is the capacity of words to be the cause of a perfect cognition that does not touch upon relation is called 'indivisibility'; or else, it is the state of having the meaning of the nominal stem [alone]. (Verse 1)
The meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] is that "having the mere sense of the nominal stem as its object" constitutes *akhaṇḍārthatva* (the state of having an impartite object).

Furthermore, that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is of two kinds: the witness of the individual soul (*jīvasākṣin*) and the witness of the Lord (*īśvarasākṣin*). Among these, the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Its witness, however, is consciousness conditioned (*upahita*) by the internal organ. The distinction between these two arises from the internal organ functioning respectively as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and as a condition (*upādhi*).

A *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier) is that which is connected with the effect and serves to differentiate; an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct), however, is that which differentiates while not being connected with the effect and exists [only as a condition]. For example, in the statement "the jar qualified by color is non-eternal," color is the *viśeṣaṇa*. In the statement "the auditory organ is the ether delimited by the ear-cavity," the ear-cavity is the *upādhi*. This very *upādhi* is called a "distinguisher" (*paricāyaka*) by the Naiyāyikas. In the present context, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is insentient, it lacks the capacity to illuminate objects; therefore, it serves as the limiting adjunct for the consciousness that illuminates objects.

Furthermore, this witness of individual life (*jīvasākṣin*) is distinct for each person; for if there were unity [of the individual witness], it would follow that when Caitra perceives something, Maitra would also have a corresponding recollection.

The witness of God (*īśvarasākṣin*), however, is consciousness conditioned by *māyā*. And that is one, because its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which is *māyā*, is one. This is justified in such scriptural passages as "Through *māyās*, Indra appears in many forms," where the plural number in "*māyābhiḥ*" is explained either as referring to specific powers residing in *māyā* or as referring to the qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—residing in *māyā*. As it is said: "One should know *māyā* to be *prakṛti*, and the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) to be the wielder of *māyā* (*māyin*)."
"Salutation to that Self of Knowledge, by fixing whom in the heart the yogi crosses over the far-reaching ignorance consisting of Māyā.
"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, who gives birth to many offspring of similar form— "
"In one unborn [Self], the other unborn [Self] lies down, enjoying her; having enjoyed his experience, he leaves her.

By such scriptural passages, the oneness of Māyā is ascertained through the force of the singular number, supported by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Consequently, the consciousness conditioned (*upahita*) by that [Māyā] is the witness of the Lord (*īśvara-sākṣin*). That [witness] is beginningless, because its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), Māyā, is beginningless. Consciousness delimited by Māyā is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). When Māyā functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is the state of being the Lord; when it functions as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is the state of being the witness. Thus, there is a distinction between the states of being the Lord and being the witness, but not a distinction between the two substrata (*dharmin*), namely the Lord and the witness.

And although that Supreme Lord is one, He assumes the designations expressed by such terms as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, according to the distinctions among the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas residing in the māyā that constitutes His own limiting adjunct (upādhi).

Now, an objection may be raised: if the Lord’s Witness is beginningless, how can the adventitious act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) attributed to the Supreme Lord at a time prior to creation—expressed in such passages as "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—be logically consistent? It is replied:

Just as various modifications (vṛtti-bhedas) arise in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), by the force of causes such as the contact between sense objects and the senses; so too, by the force of the karma of the living beings being created, specific modifications arise in Māyā, which is the limiting adjunct of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). These take the form: "This must now be created," "This must now be protected," and "This must now be withdrawn. And because these modifications have a beginning in time (sāditva), the Consciousness reflected therein is also said to be "beginningless" [only in a relative sense].

Thus, by means of the two-fold nature of the witness (sākṣin), the two-fold nature of perceptual knowledge is established. Furthermore, perceptuality (pratyakṣatva) residing in the object of knowledge has been described. In that regard, the general definition of perceptuality residing in the cognition itself is simply "consciousness" (cittva). This is because even in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire," the consciousness conditioned by the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of fire is perceptible with respect to its own self-aspect by virtue of being self-luminous. As for its perceptuality with respect to the respective objective aspect, it is exactly as previously stated.

Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of this definition to erroneous perception (*bhrāntirūpa-pratyakṣa*), because by defining "perception" as a general category common to both error and valid knowledge (*pramā*), that [erroneous perception] is also included within the scope of the definition. However, when the definition must be stated specifically for valid perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣapramā*), then it should be understood that "uncontradictedness" (*abādhitatva*) is a qualification of the object (*viṣaya-viśeṣaṇa*) in the previously mentioned definition. Since illusions such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell have as their objects illusory silver (*prātibhāsika-rajata*) and the like—which are subject to sublation (*bādha*) at some point during the course of transmigratory existence—they lack the aforementioned definition and thus there is no over-extension.

If it is argued: "Even if illusory cognition is established by means of unsuccessful activity (*visaṃvādipravṛtti*), it cannot be considered valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) if its object is the silver produced at that very moment which is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), because it is possible for the object to be the silver existing in another place, which is already established"—we say: no. For that [silver] cannot be an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) since it is not in sensory contact (*asannikṛṣṭa*). Nor can cognition itself be the means of connection (*pratyāsatti*); for if cognition were the means of connection, fire and other such objects would become perceptible through that very cognition, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the abolition of inference (*anumāna*) and other means of knowledge.

If it is objected: "In the absence of silver atoms and other such factors that produce real silver, how can even for you silver be produced upon a mother-of-pearl shell?", it is replied: The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces illusory silver is not the same as that established in common worldly experience; rather, it is entirely distinct. To explain: for one whose eyes are afflicted by defects such as cataracts (*kāca*), there arises from contact with the object present before them a certain modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of "this" and in the form of shimmering luster (*cākacakyākārā*). And within that modification, consciousness delimited by the "this" portion (*idamaṃśāvacchinna-caitanya*) is reflected.

In this regard, according to the manner previously stated, through the outward projection of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), the consciousness delimited by the "this" portion (*idamaṃśāvacchinna-caitanya*), the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛttyavacchinna-caitanya*), and the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛ-caitanya*) become non-different. Consequently, the ignorance residing in the object-consciousness—which is non-different from the knower's consciousness—characterized by the mode of "shell-ness," aided by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of silver awakened by the perception of similarity such as glittering luster, and conjoined with defects such as ophthalmia, undergoes transformation into the form of the object, namely silver, and into the form of the illusory cognition of silver.

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the attainment of the state of an effect possessing the same degree of reality as its material cause (*upādāna*). Illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is the attainment of the state of an effect possessing a different degree of reality than its material cause. Apparent silver is called a "transformation" with respect to ignorance (*avidyā*), and an "illusory manifestation" with respect to pure consciousness (*caitanya*). Furthermore, that silver, which is of the nature of a transformation of ignorance, exists within the consciousness delimited by the "this" (*idam*) which serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for ignorance. This is because, in our view, it is a necessary rule that every effect depends upon the substrate of ignorance that is its own material cause.

But how can silver, which resides in consciousness (*caitanya*), have identity with the object present before one, as expressed in the cognition "this is silver"? It is said in reply: Just as in the Nyāya system pleasure and the like, though residing in the self (*ātman*), are perceived as residing in the body because the body serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the locus of that pleasure, so too, since pure consciousness alone cannot be the substrate for silver, the consciousness delimited by "this" (*idam-avacchinna-caitanya*) is its substrate; thus, through "this" acting as the delimiting factor, there arises the cognition of the connection between silver and the object present before one.

This is logically consistent. Since that consciousness of the object is non-different from the consciousness conditioned by that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the silver superimposed upon the consciousness of the object is also superimposed upon the witness-consciousness (sākṣin); thus it is said to be "cognizable by the witness alone" and "not cognizable by any other, like pleasure and so forth."

If it is argued that, were [the object] superimposed upon the Witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), there would be the cognition "I am silver," just as there is the cognition "I am happy," we reply: It is not the case that the cognition "I am happy" is caused by the fact that pleasure and so forth are effects of ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This is because pleasure and so forth are superimposed upon pure consciousness itself, just like a jar or other objects. Rather, for whatever thing is an effect of ignorance aided by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of a certain form, that thing becomes the object of an experience of that same form.

Thus, this is the determining factor that follows [the rule]. And so, because it is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*) assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of the form "this" (*idam-ākāra*), objects such as a jar are the objects of the experience of the form "this"; because it is an effect of ignorance assisted by the latent impressions deposited by the experience of the form "I" (*aham-ākāra*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are the objects of the experience of the form "I"; and because it is an effect of ignorance assisted by the latent impressions deposited by both kinds of experience, the body, the senses, and so forth are the objects of both kinds of experience.

And thus there is a twofold experience: "this is the ear" and "I am deaf. In the present case, although illusory silver is an effect of ignorance residing in the limited consciousness (*idam-avacchinna-caitanya*) which is non-different from the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛ-caitanya*), it must be understood that it possesses the objectivity of the experience of the form "this" (*idam-ākāra*), because it is produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) left by the experience of the form "this" in a real instance such as "this is silver"; it does not, however, possess the objectivity of the experience of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form "I am silver."

If it is asked: "Even so, since illusory silver can appear by virtue of its direct relation to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), for what purpose is the postulation of an *avidyā*-modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of a semblance of cognition (*jñānābhāsa*) directed toward silver?"—it is replied: It is postulated because the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of the silver is established through its having the nature of objective immediacy, which consists in the absence of having an existence distinct from the consciousness conditioned by a modification whose object is itself.

If it is objected: "In this case, since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and the mental modification having the form of silver each have their own distinct objects, how can an erroneous cognition (*bhrama-jñāna*) be established if one accepts a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*), as the Guru [Prabhākara] does? — We reply: No. This is because we accept its status as an error on the grounds that a single consciousness reflected in two modifications simultaneously apprehends the identity between a real and an unreal object. For this very reason, the traditional teachers state that the knowledge of the Witness (*sākṣijñāna*) lacks the necessity of being valid (*prāmāṇya*), since its objects may be either real or unreal.

If it is objected: "In your own system (*siddhānta*), even silver located in another place is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*) and is superimposed (*adhyasta*); how then is there a distinction between shell-silver and that [other-place silver]?"—we reply: No. For in your view, even though there is no difference in their reality (*satyatva*), whatever factor serves as the regulator for some things being momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and others being enduring (*sthāyitva*)—namely, a particular intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) and so forth—is exactly the same for me as well.

Alternatively, in the case of the superimposition of a jar and so forth, ignorance alone is the cause by way of being a defect; however, in the case of the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl, defects such as ophthalmia and the like are also involved. Thus, being produced by adventitious defects is the determining factor for being of a phenomenal (prātibhāsika) nature. For this very reason, the chariots and other objects perceived in dreams possess a phenomenal nature because they are produced by the adventitious defect of sleep.

If it be objected: "In the case of a dream, since the practical activity [of the dreamer] is accounted for by the mere recollection of previously experienced chariots and so forth, there is no need to postulate the creation of chariots and such, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava)," we reply: No. For if one were to admit that the chariot and so forth are merely remembered, it would contradict such experiences as "I see a chariot" or "I saw a chariot in a dream. Furthermore, it would contradict the scriptural text which teaches the creation of chariots and so forth: "Then he creates chariots, horses, and roads. Therefore, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the chariots and other objects perceived in a dream are also merely illusory (prātibhāsika) and persist only as long as the illusion lasts.

If it is objected: "Since a specific location is perceived as the substratum for the chariot and so forth in a dream, one must admit an indefinable, phenomenal location that is proximate at that time; and if that is so, where does the superimposition occur?"—[the answer is: because self-luminous consciousness itself is the substratum for the chariot and so forth. For the chariot and such, when they are perceived, are perceived simply as "existing"; thus, consciousness alone, manifesting in the form of existence (*sadrūpa*), is the substratum.

The specific location as well is superimposed upon consciousness and is merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*); even the perceptibility by the senses in the case of the chariot and so forth is phenomenal, because at that time all the senses have ceased their activity. As for the production of the cognition "I am an elephant," that must be refuted as previously explained. Some hold that dream-elephants and the like are direct transformations of *māyā*; others hold that they are transformations of that [māyā] through the medium of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Objection: If elephants and the like are superimposed upon pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), then because that [consciousness] is not directly perceived at this time, would the elephants and so forth obtained in a dream persist even during the waking state? Reply: It is said: The destruction of an effect is indeed twofold. One occurs together with its material cause (*upādāna*); the other, however, occurs while the material cause still exists. The former is sublation (*bādha*); the latter is mere cessation (*nivṛtti*). The cause of the former is the direct realization of the reality of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva-sākṣātkāra*), for without that, the ignorance (*avidyā*) which constitutes the material cause is not removed.

In the second case, there is the arising of a contradictory cognition and the cessation of the defect. Therefore, here, since there is an absence of the realization of Brahman, let the dream-phenomenon not be sublated [by mere waking]. What contradiction is there in the cessation of the elephant and so forth—either through the emergence of another contradictory cognition, like that of a jar by the blow of a mallet, or through the destruction of the defect such as sleep which produced it? And thus, in the view that the silver in the shell is the effect of *tūlāvidyā* residing in the consciousness limited by the shell, the sublation of the silver occurs along with its ignorance (*ajñāna*) by the cognition "this is shell."

In the view that [the silver] is an effect of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), however, since root-ignorance is removable only by the direct realization of Brahman, its cessation there [in the case of the shell-silver] occurs merely through the cognition of the shell, just as a jar is destroyed by a blow from a mallet.

If it is objected: "If one accepts the existence of the silver as *pratibhāsika* (illusory appearance) at the time of its manifestation in the shell, then the cognition of a threefold negation—'this is not silver'—would not occur; rather, it would be 'now this is not silver,' just like 'now the jar is not black,'" we reply: No. For in that case, the object of the negative cognition is not an absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by the property of "silver-ness."

However, this is because we accept the existence of an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇadharma), specifically an absence whose counter-correlate is illusory silver delimited by both empirical and ultimate reality.

Now, one might ask: is ultimate reality apprehended in the illusory silver or not? If it is not apprehended, the perception of the absence cannot occur due to the lack of knowledge of the counter-correlate as delimited by its delimiting property (pratiyogitāvacchedaka). If it is apprehended, then since the cause of immediate manifestation is necessarily dependent on the existence of the object at that very time [and illusory silver lacks such existence], [the perception of its absence would be impossible].

If it is asked: "Since even the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of the silver has arisen as something indefinable just like the silver itself, how can the absence of that [silver] delimited by ultimate reality exist there when the existence of the silver delimited by that [reality] is present?"—we say: no. This is because we do not admit the production of ultimate reality residing in the silver, since ultimate reality, which resides in the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), can only appear [as such] in the silver. For it is accepted that the production of a phenomenal object (*prātibhāsika-vastu*) occurs only where the superimposed object is not in sensory contact. It is for this very reason that the redness residing in a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) does not arise [in the crystal] through sensory contact.

If it is argued that, in such a case as where a hibiscus flower is not in close proximity due to the intervention of another substance, one must therefore accept that the redness perceived there is merely illusory (prātibhāsika), we say no, because this is actually desired [by us]. Likewise, in other perceptual errors as well, one should demonstrate the presence of the definition of "correct perception" (yathārtha-pratyakṣa) while still conforming to the general definition of perception.

It has been stated that perception is of two kinds according to another classification: that produced by the sense organs and that not produced by them. Among these, the perception of pleasure and so forth that is not produced by the sense organs belongs to the mind; as for the perception of pleasure and so forth produced by the sense organs, it belongs to the mind because the status of the mind as a sense organ has been refuted.

The five sense organs consist of the nose, tongue, eye, ear, and skin. All sense organs produce perceptual knowledge only when they are in contact with their respective objects. Among them, the sense organs consisting of the nose, tongue, and skin produce the apprehension of odor, taste, and touch while remaining in their own locations. The eye and the ear, however, go to the location of the object itself and grasp their respective objects.

Since the auditory organ, like the eyes and other senses, is limited in extent, it is possible for it to reach the location of the drum and such; hence the experience: "The sound of the drum has been heard by me. [Otherwise], there would be the complexity of postulating the production of an infinite number of sounds in the region of the ear-cavity according to the analogy of waves and ripples, as well as the complexity of postulating that the direct perception "the sound of the drum has been heard by me" is an error. Thus has perception been explained. This concludes the second chapter, on Perception, in the *Śrīmad-Vedānta-paribhāṣā*.

Now, inference (*anumāna*) is defined. Inference is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inferential cognition (*anumiti*). And inferential cognition is produced by the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), insofar as it has the nature of being the knowledge of pervasion. Since the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of the knowledge of pervasion and the like are not produced by that [knowledge of pervasion] in its specific nature, they do not possess the status of inferential cognition. Furthermore, the instrument of inferential cognition is the knowledge of pervasion, and its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). However, the third consideration of the mark (*tṛtīyaliṅgaparāmarśa*) is not the instrument for inferential cognition; because its status as a cause of inferential cognition is unestablished, its status as the instrument is dismissed far and wide.

Nor does it follow that an inference would incur the status of being a memory simply because it is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). This is because the defining condition for memory is either being produced by the prior absence of memory or being produced by a mental impression alone; therefore, being produced by a mental impression in general—which is common even to the destruction of a mental impression—is not a sufficient condition for it to be a memory. Furthermore, one should not ask how a mental impression can be the cause of an inference in cases where the inference arises from the recollection of a pervasion (*vyāpti*); for even when the root is the recollection of pervasion, it is precisely the mental impression of that [pervasion] which serves as the cause of the inference.

There is no rule that memory necessarily destroys its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), for we observe the occurrence of a continuous stream of memories. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of inference arising from an unawakened impression, because the awakening of that impression itself serves as a necessary auxiliary condition. Thus, when there is the cognition of the subject's possession of the property (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*)—namely, "this possesses smoke"—and the awakening of the impression deposited by the experience "smoke is pervaded by fire," the inference "it possesses fire" occurs. One need not postulate an intermediate recollection of the pervasion (*vyāptismaraṇa*), nor a cognition qualified by that [pervasion] such as "this possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," as a cause of inference; for such a view is cumbersome (*gaurava*) and lacks supporting evidence (*mānābhāva*).

And that cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) only with respect to the portion of the cognition whose object is fire, and not with respect to the cognition whose object is the mountain; for in the cognition "the mountain possesses fire," the character of inference (*anumititva*) resides only in the portion concerning fire, not in the portion concerning the mountain, since it has been established that the latter portion is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, pervasion consists in the state of having a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) as it subsists in all substrata of the probans (*sādhana*).

And that [invariable concomitance] is grasped through the observation of coexistence once the knowledge of deviation has been excluded. As for whether that observation of coexistence consists of repeated observations or a single observation, no distinction need be emphasized, since the mere observation of coexistence is what is causally effective.

Furthermore, this inference is exclusively of the *anvayi* (positive) type, and not *kevalānvayi* (purely positive). This is because, in our view, every property whatsoever is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in Brahman; thus, the status of being *kevalānvayi*—defined as having a probandum that is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence—is unestablished.

Nor does inference possess the nature of a negative (vyatireki) inference, because the knowledge of pervasion defined by the absence of the probans when the probandum is absent is of no use for the inferential cognition of the probandum by means of the probans. How then, one might ask, can there be an inferential cognition from the knowledge of negative pervasion even for one who does not know the positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) in the case of smoke and so forth? We shall explain that it is through the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). For this very reason, inference does not possess the nature of both positive and negative pervasion, since the knowledge of negative pervasion is not a cause of inferential cognition.

That inference is of two kinds, distinguished as *svārtha* (for one's own sake) and *parārtha* (for the sake of others). Among these, *svārtha* has already been explained. *Parārtha*, however, is accomplished by means of *nyāya*. *Nyāya* is defined as a collection of members (*avayava*). The members are exactly three, either in the form of proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*udāharaṇa*), or in the form of example, application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*). They do not consist of five members, because since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) can be demonstrated by just three members, the two additional members would be redundant.

Thus, inference having been examined, the falsity of the entire phenomenal world as distinct from Brahman is established. To explain: everything distinct from Brahman is false, because it is distinct from Brahman; whatever is thus is so, just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Nor is the example unestablished, for that has already been proven. Nor is the reason (hetu) irrelevant, because in the case of the falsity of the silver in a shell, the rope-snake, and so forth, the property of being distinct from Brahman is the most parsimonious (laghava) cause of their falsity.

Falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in everything that is intended as its own substratum (*svāśraya*). The word "intended" (*abhimata*) is for the purpose of excluding impossibility (*asambhava*); the word "everything" (*yāvat*) is for the purpose of excluding other [unwanted] meanings (*arthāntara*). As it has been said: "For all entities whatsoever, insofar as they are accepted as their own substratum, the state of being false consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence."

Alternatively, the following inference is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for [establishing] falsity: "This cloth is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in these very threads, because it is a cloth, like another cloth. As it has been said:

"The whole (*aṃśin*) is the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence residing in its own parts, because it is a whole, just like other wholes; this same direction [of argument] applies to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth as well."

Nor does the falsity of the jar and so forth entail the contradiction of perception by the cognition "the jar exists," because the existence of the substrate-Brahman is the object there, and thus the reality of the jar and so forth is not established. Nor should it be argued how formless Brahman can be the object of visual or other sensory cognitions; for even formless things such as color (as a quality) are perceived. Furthermore, there is no rule that a formless substance is unfit for perception by the eyes and other senses, since in my view the status of Brahman as a substance is not established.

It is your position that substantiality (*dravyatva*) consists in being the locus of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*) or being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*); however, Brahman, being devoid of qualities, cannot be the locus of qualities, nor can it be an inherent cause, since inherence (*samavāya*) is not established. Or, even if Brahman were to possess substantiality, there would still be no contradiction in its being an object of visual and other forms of cognition, just as time—which is formless—is [an object of such cognition].

Alternatively, existence (*sattva*) is threefold: absolute existence (*pāramārthika-sattva*), which belongs to Brahman; empirical existence (*vyāvahārika-sattva*), which belongs to space and so forth; and apparent existence (*pratibhāsika-sattva*), which belongs to the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. Thus, the validity of the perception "the jar exists" is established by its having empirical existence as its object. And on this view, the negation of the jar and other such things in Brahman does not occur in their own nature, but only in terms of absolute existence; therefore, there is no contradiction.

And in this definition of falsity (*mithyātva*), it should be understood that "having a counter-correlativity delimited by ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*) is a qualification of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Therefore, the inference of falsity is established.
Thus ends the second chapter, on Inference, in the *Śrīmad-Vedānta-paribhāṣā*.

Now, analogy (upamāna) is being defined. In this context, analogy is the instrument for the valid cognition of similarity. To illustrate: when a person who has previously seen a cow in a courtyard goes to the forest and comes into sensory contact with a gavaya, there arises the cognition, "This animal is similar to a cow. Immediately thereafter, there occurs the certain conclusion, "My cow is similar to this [gavaya]. In this process, by means of positive and negative concomitance, the cognition of the similarity of the cow residing in the gavaya is the instrument (karaṇa), and the cognition of the similarity of the gavaya residing in the cow is the result (phala).

Nor can this [recognition] occur through perception, because at that time the cow-individual is not in contact with the senses; nor can it occur through inference, because the similarity residing in the gavaya is not a valid logical mark (*liṅga*) for it. Nor should it be argued that its occurrence is possible through the following inference: "My cow is similar to this gavaya, because it is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the similarity residing in this [gavaya]; whatever is the counter-correlative of a similarity residing in something is similar to that thing, just as Caitra, being the counter-correlative of the similarity residing in Maitra, is similar to Maitra."

Even in the absence of such an inference, because the cognition "my cow is similar to this one" is established by experience, and because there is a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "I am cognizing through comparison," therefore comparison (*upamāna*) is a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus ends the section on comparison in the *Vedāntaparibhāṣā*. 3.

Now, verbal testimony (*āgama*) is examined. A sentence is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when the relation that constitutes its intended meaning (*tātparya*) is not sublated by any other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, there are four causes for the cognition produced by a sentence: expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), contiguity (*āsatti*), and the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparyajñāna*).

In this context, *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is the fitness of word-meanings to become objects of mutual inquiry (*jijñāsā*). This is because when an action (*kriyā*) is heard, there arises a desire to know its factors (*kāraka*), and when those are heard, there is a desire to know the action; likewise, when an instrument (*karaṇa*) is heard, there is a desire to know the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Even for one who does not have such a desire, the fitness for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is included. And since the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of that fitness are "being an action," "being a factor," and so forth, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Furthermore, in cases of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) such as "cow, horse, man, elephant," the delimiter is "being expressed by words with identical case-endings"; thus, there is no non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

It is precisely with this intention regarding such expectancy that, in the *Balābalādhikaraṇa*, there is the conventional usage in the passage "That curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) belongs to the Viśvedevas; [the whey] (*vājina*) belongs to the Vājins," stating that because the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is already connected with the *āmikṣā*, it has no expectancy for the *vājina*. If it is argued: "Even in that case, although the *vājina* is not the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), it certainly possesses the capacity for it, since being a substance to be offered (*pradeyadravyatva*) is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the capacity to be the object of the desire to know as defined by the sacrifice"—we say: No.

Since the property of being a substance to be offered (*pradeyadravyatva*)—concomitant with the absence of a cognition of connection with a substance of its own class—is the very delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of that [connection], whereas the whey-substance (*vājina*) is concomitant with a cognition of connection with a substance of its own class and thus lacks such a delimiting character; whereas this is not the case for the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), because at that time there is no presentation of a connection with the whey.
In other examples as well, it should be understood that the lack of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣāviraha*) alone is the weak motivator.

And *yogyatā* (semantic competency) is the non-sublation (*abādha*) of the relation that constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparyaviṣaya*). In cases such as "one should sprinkle with fire," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because such a relation is sublated. Even in passages such as "That Prajāpati extracted his own omentum," there is semantic competency because the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the animal sacrifice—which is the object of the intention—is not sublated. Furthermore, in sentences such as "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*), although there is sublation of the difference between the literal meanings (*vācyābhedabādha*), there is semantic competency because there is no sublation of the identity of the essential nature (*lakṣyasvarūpābheda*) [of the two referents].

Proximity (*āsatti*) is the presentation of word-meanings by words without intervention. The phrase "generated by words" (*padajanyā*) is used because there is no comprehension of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for a word-meaning presented through other means of knowledge (*māna*). For this very reason, in cases where a word-meaning has not been heard, that specific word must be supplied (*adhyāhāra*), as in "close the door" (*pidhehi*) in the case of "the door" (*dvāram*); likewise, in "for the sake of *iṣ*, thee" (*iṣe tvā*), the word "cut" (*chinadmi*) is supplied; and for this same reason, in the modified rituals (*vikṛti*), the expression "I offer what is pleasing to Sūrya" (*sūryāya juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) is employed.

The meaning of a word (*padārtha*) is twofold: the denotable (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). Among these, "denotation" (*śakti*) is the primary function of words with respect to their meanings. For example, the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) has its function in a particular object characterized by a shape such as a broad base and a belly. And this denotation is a distinct category of reality (*padārthāntara*), because in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the mere capacity conducive to an effect within causes is considered a distinct category of reality. Furthermore, that [denotation] is to be inferred from the effect, which consists in the knowledge of the word-meaning produced by each respective word. Being the object of such a capacity is "denotability" (*śakyatva*).

And that [denotation] belongs to the universal alone, not to the individual, because individuals are too numerous and thus cumbersome. If it is asked, "How then does the cognition of the individual arise from words such as 'cow'?", we reply: it is through the universal being cognized by the same cognition as the individual.

Alternatively, the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" resides in the individual (*vyakti*) by its very existence (*svarūpasatī*), but not as something cognized; whereas in the case of the universal (*jāti*), that power is the cause [of comprehension] precisely because it is cognized. Furthermore, the cognition of the power with respect to the individual is not a cause, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). Moreover, once the cognition of the possession of power in the universal exists, there is no delay in the cognition of the individual even without the cognition of power in the individual. For this very reason, even in the Nyāya system, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the power resides in the relation (*anvaya*) by its very existence. Since being the denoted object (*vācyatva*) consists solely in being the object of the cognition of power, it is the universal alone that is denoted.

Alternatively, there is comprehension through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual (*vyakti*). Just as in the expression "blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), the word "blue" has an indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is qualified by the quality of blueness, so too a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) has an indicative function with respect to that which is qualified by it. As it has been said: "The meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise. Thus, the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) has been defined.

Now, the denoted object (*lakṣya*) is defined. In this context, the *lakṣya* is the object of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Indication is of two kinds: primary indication (*kevalalakṣaṇā*) and indicated-indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*). Among these, primary indication is the direct relationship with the primary meaning (*śakya*). For example, in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," there is primary indication of the word "Gaṅgā" for the bank, which is directly related to the current. Where there is the cognition of another meaning through a mediated relationship with the primary meaning, there is indicated-indication.

Just as the word *dvirepha*—which possesses the power (*śakti*) to denote two *repha*s (the letter *r*)—functions with respect to a bee through a traditional connection (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of its being part of the word *bhramara*;

so too, secondary indication (*gauṇī*) is indeed a case of "indication by indication" (*lakṣita-lakṣaṇā*). For example, in the expression "The boy is a lion," the boy is understood through his connection with qualities such as cruelty, which belong to that which is denoted by the word "lion.
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is of three kinds according to another classification: *jahat-lakṣaṇā*, *ajahat-lakṣaṇā*, and *jahad-ajahat-lakṣaṇā*.

*Jahat-lakṣaṇā* (indication with abandonment) occurs where another meaning is understood without including the primary sense; for example, "Eat poison. For here, having abandoned its own meaning, the word indicates the cessation of eating at the house of an enemy. *Ajahat-lakṣaṇā* (indication without abandonment) occurs where another meaning is understood while including the primary sense itself; for example, "A white jar. For here, the word "white," having included its own meaning—the quality of whiteness—functions by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote the substance possessing that quality.

For where a word denoting a qualified entity (viśiṣṭavācaka-śabda) functions with respect to one part [of its meaning] while abandoning another part of its own referent, there is the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*. For example, "This is that Devadatta. Here, because the identity of the two qualified entities expressed by the two words is logically untenable, both words have as their primary purport only the substantive (viśeṣyamātra).

Or, for instance, in cases such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the traditional teachers maintain that because the referent of the word *tat*—qualified by omniscience and so forth—is not identical with the referent of the word *tvam*—qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—there must be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) in order to establish their identity.

We, however, say this: in such cases as "This Devadatta, you are that" (*so 'yaṃ devadattas tattvam asi*), even though words denoting qualified entities refer only to a part [of their meaning], there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For when the non-occurrence of the identity relation between two qualified entities—presented through their primary powers (*śakti*)—is untenable, there is no contradiction in the cognition of the relation between the two substrata (*viśeṣya*) themselves, which are indeed presented through their primary powers. This is just as in the case of "The pot is impermanent," where, although the potness (*ghaṭatva*) denoted by a portion of the word "pot" is unfit [to be the locus of impermanence], the impermanence is related to the individual pot (*ghaṭavyakti*) which is fit.

Where there is a presentation of a portion of a word-meaning as a qualifier, it is precisely for the sake of its independent presentation that metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is accepted; for example, in the sentence "The pot is eternal," since the property of potness (ghaṭatva) is not independently presented by the power of the word "pot" (through primary denotation), metaphorical indication is attributed to the word "pot" with respect to potness in order to achieve such a presentation. In the same way, there is no metaphorical indication even in sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), because there is no obstacle to the syntactic relation of identity between the referents of the words "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam), both of which are independently presented by their own powers.

Otherwise, in cases such as "the pot is in the house," "color is in the pot," or "bring the pot," since the potness, houseness, and so forth would be capable of being understood through the intended syntactic connection, the words "pot" and the like would have to refer to the substantive alone through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) even there. Therefore, the teachers' mention of secondary signification regarding the sentence "That thou art" should be understood as a concessionary argument (abhyupagamavāda). The example of the "partially abandoning and partially not abandoning" secondary signification (jahadajahallakṣaṇā), however, is indeed "Let the curd be protected from crows" and the like; for in that case, the word "crow" applies both to non-crows and to crows by excluding the denoted crow and by taking into account the quality of being a destroyer of curd, which is not denoted.

The ground for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), however, is precisely the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*), and not the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*). This is because in the case of "Let them protect the curd from crows," there is no impossibility of syntactic connection; whereas in cases such as "A hamlet on the Ganges," the impossibility of the intended meaning is indeed possible. Furthermore, secondary signification does not reside in a word alone, but also in a sentence; for example, in "A hamlet on the deep river," the secondary signification of "on the bank" belongs to the entire collection of the two words "deep" and "river."

[Objection: But how can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in a relation with what is possible [to denote], through a sentence that lacks such power? [Reply: It is said: Indication is the relation with that which is made known by the connection of a word through its primary power (*śakti*). And just as the meaning of a word is made known by the primary power, so too is the meaning of a sentence; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. In this way, for explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) consisting of praise, there is indication in the sense of "praiseworthiness" (*prāśastya*); for explanatory passages of censure such as "He wept," there is indication in the sense of "censurability" (*ninditatva*).

If one were to accept that words occurring in an *arthavāda* possess *lakṣaṇā* (indication) with respect to excellence (*prāśastya*), then, since that [excellence] could be presented by a single word through *lakṣaṇā*, the other words would be redundant.

Thus, because the collection of words in an *arthavāda* functions as a substitute for a single word—by conveying the meaning of excellence required by the injunction—it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunctive word; this is what is meant by the "word-level syntactical unity" (*padaikavākyatā*) of *arthavāda* sentences.

Where, then, does syntactic unity between sentences (*vākyaikavākyatā*) occur? It occurs where two sentences, each expressing a distinct relation, come to convey the meaning of a larger sentence (*mahāvākya*) by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For example, there is syntactic unity between the sentences "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*) and the sentences "He offers the *samidh* oblation" (*samidho yajati*), because they mutually convey the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). As the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda has said: "Sentences that are complete in conveying their own respective meanings [attain unity] through the requirement of the relationship of principal and subordinate."
Furthermore, the unity of sentences arises from their being combined together. Thus [it is said].

Thus, the two kinds of word-meanings have been defined. Their presentation is proximity (*āsatti*). And that [proximity] is a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is observed in that very manner. Likewise, in the case of the comprehension of the meaning of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the comprehension of the meaning of the subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) is the cause, because positive and negative concomitance is ascertained in that very way.

The *tātparya* (intentional import), which follows in the sequence, is now defined. In this regard, *tātparya* is not simply "being uttered with the desire for that [specific] cognition," because it would follow that no meaning would appear from the Veda when uttered by a person devoid of knowledge of its meaning; furthermore, even the delusion regarding *tātparya* would be absent due to the perception of the particularity that "this teacher is unlearned. Nor should it be said that verbal comprehension occurs there through the knowledge of God’s *tātparya*, since we observe the apprehension of the meaning of those sentences even by one who does not accept God. It is replied: [The definition is: *Tātparya* is the intention (*vivakṣā*) of the speaker. This is because, even if a word is uttered with the desire to convey a certain meaning, if the speaker has no intention regarding another meaning, no verbal comprehension arises in respect to that other meaning. Nor is there any fault in the definition, for the intention of the speaker is known through the context, the capacity of the words, and so forth. As for the objection that there would be no *tātparya* in the case of the Veda, since it was not uttered by a human, it is answered: the Veda is indeed the utterance of God, and thus its *tātparya* is established. Or, let us assume the Veda is eternal; nevertheless, its *tātparya* is determined by the intention of the person who explains it. Therefore, *tātparya* is the intention of the speaker. And this intention is grasped through the aforementioned means. Thus, the definition is flawless. Furthermore, the intention of the speaker is not something distinct from the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), because the two are identical in nature. Hence, *tātparya* is nothing but the desire to speak. And this desire is inferred from the resulting verbal comprehension. Thus, everything is consistent. ||| End of Chapter 2 ||| (Note: The bracketed portion provides the formal definition and resolution of objections based on the provided Sanskrit text.)

Tātparya (intentional import) is the capacity to generate the cognition of that [specific relation]. For instance, the sentence "There is a jar in the house" has the capacity to generate the cognition of the relation between the jar and the house, but not the capacity to generate the cognition of the relation between the cloth and the house; therefore, that sentence is designated as being "intent upon" the relation with the jar, and not "intent upon" the relation with the cloth.

If it is objected: "Even when a sentence such as 'Bring the Saindhava' is uttered with the intention of producing the cognition of bringing salt, since its capacity for generating the cognition of a connection with a horse exists by its very nature, there would follow the cognition of a connection with a horse even at the time when the sentence is intended to refer to salt"—we reply: No. This is because the condition of not being uttered with the intention of producing a cognition other than that [specific one] is also a qualifier of *tātparya* (speaker's intention).
