Furthermore, a sentence is said to be "intended for the connection" (*saṃsarga-para*) with respect to a certain object when, while being capable of generating the cognition of that object, it is not uttered out of a desire to produce the cognition of something else. This definition applies even to the speech of parrots and the like, as well as to Vedic sentences uttered by those who have not mastered the language; since there is an absence of any desire to produce the cognition of that [other] object, and thus an absence of being uttered out of a desire to produce the cognition of something else, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Nor is there a lack of pervasion in the case of a sentence uttered out of a desire to produce the cognitions of both [the primary and the secondary], because what is intended here is the state of not being uttered out of a desire to produce the cognition of *only* that other thing.

And the capacity (*śakti*) is that which delimits the fitness for producing the aforementioned mere cognition. In our view, however, since it is the capacity alone that delimits causality in every case, there is no fault whatsoever.

Thus, once it is established that intention (*tātparya*), consisting in the capacity to produce that cognition, is the producer of verbal knowledge, the statement in the fourth section (*varṇaka*) which refutes intention as a cause of verbal knowledge is intended to refute intention in the sense of "being uttered with the desire to produce that cognition"; otherwise, it would follow that the inquiry into the Vedānta—which has the ascertainment of intention as its fruit—would be useless.

However, some maintain that the statement in the fourth section (*caturthavarṇaka*) intends to show that the knowledge of intention (*tātparyajñāna*) is not a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) in its general form as such; rather, the knowledge of intention is indeed a cause specifically for those instances of verbal cognition that follow a doubt or error regarding the intention. For, when there is a doubt regarding the intention—such as "Does this sentence intend this meaning, or another?"—or when there is an error regarding it, the subsequent ascertainment of the sentence-meaning is impossible without the ascertainment of the intention. Furthermore, they say that in the case of the Veda, that intention is determined solely through the logic refined by Mīmāṃsā, whereas in common worldly usage, it is determined through context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors.

In that regard, worldly sentences possess the character of restatement (*anuvādakatva*) because their objects are already known through other means of knowledge. In the Veda, however, there is no restatement because the meaning of the sentence is something previously unknown (*apūrva*).

In both the world and the Veda, even sentences concerning established facts (*siddhārtha*) possess authority due to their being previously unknown, just like those concerned with what is to be accomplished (*kārya*); for instance, because the capacity of words is determined even in established facts such as "A son is born to you" or "Your daughter is pregnant. For this very reason, the Vedānta sentences possess authority regarding Brahman. How this is so will be explained in the section on the subject matter (*viṣayapariccheda*).

Regarding this, the Naiyāyikas maintain that the authority of the Vedāntas derives from their being perceived by the eternal, omniscient Supreme Lord. The Mīmāṃsakas hold that the authority of the Vedas arises from their eternity, which excludes all human defects. In our view, however, the Veda is not eternal because it possesses an origin; its having an origin is established by such scriptural passages as, "The Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda are the breath of this Great Being. Nor do the Vedas possess a duration of only three moments.

This is because it would contradict such recognitions as, "The very same Veda that was studied by Devadatta has been studied by me as well. For this very reason, even the phonemes such as the letter *ga* are not momentary, because that would contradict the recognition, "This is that same letter *ga*. Thus, the Veda—as a collection of phonemes, words, and sentences—possesses an origination at the time of creation, like the ether and other elements, and is the counter-positive of destruction at the time of dissolution; however, there is no origination or destruction of the phonemes in the interim, due to the complexity (gaurava) involved in postulating an infinite number of distinct *ga*-phonemes.

The non-manifestation of phonemes (*varṇa*) during the state of non-utterance is not contradictory, as it results from the absence of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) consisting of their utterance, just like the non-perception of a jar situated in darkness. As for the perception that "the letter *ga* has arisen" and so forth, it is either invalid due to its contradiction with the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that same letter *ga*," or it is valid only insofar as it refers to a mediated relationship (*paramparāsambandha*) defined by the production residing in the sounds (*dhvani*) that manifest the phonemes. Therefore, the Vedas are not momentary.

If it is argued: "But even if momentariness is absent, since [the Vedas] possess origination like the cosmic manifestation of ether and so forth, they would be the work of the Supreme Lord; thus, your own tenet that the Vedas are not of human origin (apauruṣeya) would be undermined"—we reply: No. For being uttered by a person does not constitute "being of human origin" (pauruṣeyatva), because even according to the Guru’s school (Prabhākara), this would result in [the Vedas] being of human origin due to the succession of teachers.

Nor does "being produced by a person" consist in having its production dependent upon a person; for if that were the case, the inference of authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*) favored by the Naiyāyikas would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by us and others. Rather, being produced by a person consists in being the object of an utterance that does not depend on a prior utterance of the same kind. Thus, at the time of the beginning of creation, the Supreme Lord composed the Veda with an order of sequence identical to the order of sequence of the Veda established in the previous creation, but not a Veda of a different kind; therefore, being produced by a person does not mean being the object of an utterance independent of a prior utterance of the same kind.

The utterances of [texts] such as the *Mahābhārata*, however, are produced without depending upon utterances of the same kind; thus, they possess human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*). In this way, scripture (*āgama*) has been described as being of two kinds, distinguished by the categories of human and non-human authorship.
Thus ends the section on scripture in the *Vedāntaparibhāṣā*. 4.

Now, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is being examined. In this context, *arthāpatti* is the postulation of a necessitating factor (*upapādaka*) through the cognition of a fact to be necessitated (*upapādya*). Here, the cognition of the fact to be necessitated is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the cognition of the necessitating factor is the result (*phala*). That which cannot be established without something else is the fact to be necessitated in that context; that in the absence of which another thing is unestablished is the necessitating factor in that context. For example, since for one who does not eat during the day, corpulence is unestablished without eating at night, such corpulence is the fact to be necessitated, and eating at night is the necessitating factor.

In the case of a cognition consisting of the conceptualization of eating at night, the term *arthāpatti* occurs as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the conceptualization (kalpanā) of an object (artha). In the case of the knowledge of fatness and so forth, which is the instrument of that conceptualization, it occurs as a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhisamāsa*) meaning "that from which there is the conceptualization of an object. Thus, that term is used for both the result and the instrument.
Furthermore, that *arthāpatti* is of two kinds: presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) and presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).

Among these, presumption based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) is as follows: when silver is apprehended in that which is present before one through the cognition "this is silver," its being negated in that very same place by the cognition "this is not silver" would be inexplicable if it were real; therefore, this [negation] leads to the postulation of the silver's falsity—its difference from reality and its possession of the absolute absence of reality.

Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is the postulation of another meaning by way of the inconsistency of the literal sense of a sentence that is being heard. For example, in the case of "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," the falsity of bondage is postulated because the fact that the collection of bonds denoted by the word "sorrow"—which is heard in the text—is something to be removed by knowledge would otherwise be inconsistent. Or, for instance, upon hearing the sentence "Devadatta, who lives for a hundred years, is not in the house," one postulates his presence outside, since the absence from the house of a living person is inconsistent [with the fact of his life].

Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is of two kinds: non-occurrence of expression (*abhidhānānupapatti*) and non-occurrence of the expressed (*abhihitānupapatti*). Among these, where, upon hearing a portion of a sentence, another word necessary for the expression of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is postulated because the expression of that relation would otherwise be impossible, there is non-occurrence of expression. For example, in the case of "the door," the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "close it" is supplied; or as in "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the ellipsis of the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) is supplied.

If it is asked: "But in cases such as 'the door' (*dvāram*), since the expression of the connection (*anvaya*) occurs first, how can there be the cognition that this expression of the connection is inexplicable without a word that brings to mind the act of closing? — we say: no. This is because, by the *karaṇa* (instrumental) derivation of the word *abhidhāna*, what is intended is the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Thus, even in that case, the following cognition is possible: "The state of being directed toward the relation between the act of closing and the object 'door' is inexplicable without a word that brings to mind the act of closing."

The "inconsistency of what has been stated" (abhihitānupapatti), however, is to be observed in cases where the meaning understood from a sentence, being recognized as inconsistent, leads to the postulation of another meaning. For example, in the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the means-to-heavenhood, as it is understood to reside in the momentary Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, is inconsistent; therefore, an intermediate transcendental result (apūrva) is postulated.

Furthermore, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) cannot be subsumed under inference (*anumāna*), because it is not included among the positive-inferential (*anvayin*) types due to the lack of knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*); as for negative-inferential (*vyatirekin*) inference, its status as inference has already been refuted. For this very reason, in the case of presumption, there is no subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of the form "I infer," but rather "I postulate this by means of that. Now, it was stated that in the case of presumption, the cognition "this is inexplicable without that" is the instrument (*karaṇa*); what, then, is this "inexplicability without that"? We reply: it is being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of that [other thing].

Thus, since presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is established as a distinct means of knowledge, negative inference (*vyatirekin*) is not a separate type of inference. This is because in cases such as "the earth is distinct from others," the cognition that "the possession of odor is otherwise inexplicable (*anupapanna*) without its distinction from others" serves as the cause [of the inferential conclusion]. For this very reason, there is a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form: "I am postulating the distinction of the earth from others. Thus ends the section on Presumptive Testimony in the *Vedāntaparibhāṣā*. (5)

Now the sixth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being defined. The means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the uncommon cause of the experience of absence that is not produced by an instrument of knowledge. The term "not produced" (*ajanya*) is included to exclude inference and other such means which are causes for the experience of supersensible absences produced by inference and so forth. The term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is included to exclude merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other common causes. The qualifier "experience" (*anubhava*) is included to exclude the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the uncommon cause of the recollection of absence.

Nor should it be argued that even in cases where non-existence is inferred, non-existence should be apprehended by non-perception alone, as there is no distinction [between the two cases]; for even when there is the presence of the non-perception of dharma and so forth, their non-existence is not ascertained, and thus it is only the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*) that apprehends non-existence.

Now, what is this "non-apprehension of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*)? Is it the non-apprehension of a perceptible counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), or is it the non-apprehension of a counter-positive in a perceptible locus (*adhikaraṇa*)? If it is the first, then the distinction of a *piśāca* (demon) and so forth from a pillar would result in being imperceptible. If it is the second, then the absence of *dharma* (merit) and so forth in the self would result in being perceptible. To this we reply: No. This is because we rely on the *karmadhāraya* compound: "that which is both perceptible and a non-apprehension. And the perceptibility of the non-apprehension consists in its having as its counter-positive that which is entailed by the assumption of the existence of the counter-positive (*tarkitapratiyogisattvaprasañjitapratiyogikatva*).

The nature of that non-apprehension which is the state of being capable of such non-apprehension (*tadanupalabdhi-yogyatvam*) is as follows: when the absence of something is apprehended, its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is hypothetically assumed to exist in the locus; that non-apprehension whose nature is the apprehension of that counter-positive—which is thus rendered possible for occurrence—is what constitutes the fitness for such non-apprehension. For instance, on a ground possessed of ample light, because the following logical consequence (*āpādana*) is possible—"If a jar were present here, then there would be the apprehension of a jar"—the absence of the jar on such a ground is cognizable through non-apprehension.

In darkness, however, because there is no possibility of producing such a [perceptual] apprehension, non-apprehension is not a means of cognition. For this very reason, if a *piśāca* were present as identical with a pillar, it would follow that it would be perceptible just like the pillar; therefore, its absence is cognizable through non-apprehension. On the other hand, even though *dharma* and *adharma* exist in the self, because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is impossible to produce the aforementioned apprehension; thus, the absence of *dharma* and so forth is not cognizable through non-apprehension.

If it is argued: "Surely, according to the reasoning already stated, you accept that in cases where there is contact between the sense organ and its locus, the non-existence (abhāva) is cognizable through non-apprehension (anupalabdhi); in that case, the sense organ itself, which is already established [as the instrument], must be the instrument even for the mental modification (vṛtti) taking the form of non-existence, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance of the sense organ"—we say no. This is because the non-apprehension of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is already established as a cause for the perception of non-existence; therefore, one need only postulate its status as an instrument.

Furthermore, because the absence of a sense faculty, along with the absence of contact, is not a cause for the apprehension of non-existence, the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) of the sense faculty are otherwise accounted for (anyathāsiddhi), being exhausted by their role in the cognition of the locus and so forth.

If it is argued: "In a case such as the experience of absence, 'There is no jar on the ground,' the perceptuality (*pratyakṣatva*) regarding the portion that is the ground is established for both [parties]; therefore, since the emergence of the mental mode (*vṛtti*) is necessary there, the consciousness delimited by the absence of the jar residing in that [ground] is non-different from the cognizer, just like the consciousness delimited by the ground; thus, even in the final system (*siddhānta*), the perceptuality of the absence of the jar is established"—this is true. However, although the cognition of absence is perceptual, its instrument, namely non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), constitutes a distinct means of knowledge (*māna*).

For it is not the case that when a cognition has reached its fruition as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its instrument must necessarily be the means of valid knowledge known as perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). This is because, even though the cognition produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is a direct perception, its instrument—the sentence—is accepted as being a means of valid knowledge distinct from perception. If it is asked: "How can there be a difference between means of valid knowledge without a difference in their results?"—the answer is: No, for a difference between means of valid knowledge is established merely through a difference in the mental modification (*vṛtti*).

And thus, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of the absence of a jar is not produced by the sense organ, because there is no sensory contact with the qualifier (the jar), which is the object; rather, it is produced by another means of knowledge consisting of the non-perception of the jar. Therefore, non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) constitutes a distinct means of knowledge.

Now, if non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) were a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then since the cognition of absence would be perceptual, even the erroneous cognition of the absence of a jar in a place where a jar is present would have to be considered perceptual. Consequently, one would have to admit an indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) absence of the jar even in that case. This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because if that [erroneous absence] were produced by *māyā*, its status as an absence (*abhāvatva*) would be untenable; and if it were not produced by *māyā*, then *māyā* could not be established as the material cause (*upādāna*) of all effects. If this is argued:

No; for the error regarding the absence of a jar in a place where a jar is present does not have as its object an absence of the jar produced at that time. Rather, it is simply the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), wherein the worldly absence of the jar existing in the nature of the ground and so forth is superposed upon the ground. This is because, in all cases involving the contact with the object of superposition, it is established that it is indeed misapprehension. Alternatively, even if one grants that in a case of error regarding the absence of something in a place where its counter-positive is present, that absence is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), nevertheless, its material cause is nothing other than *māyā*.

For there is no absolute homogeneity between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), since even in the case of threads and cloth, there is heterogeneity by virtue of their respective natures as "thread-ness" and "cloth-ness. There exists at least some degree of homogeneity, given that Māyā—the indefinable cause—is present in the form of the property of falsity (*mithyātva*) belonging to the absence of a jar. Otherwise, why would you not raise the doubt: "How can Māyā be the material cause of the empirical absence of a jar? Nor should it be argued that if the relation of material cause and effect could exist between heterogeneous things, then Brahman alone would be the material cause of the world.

This is because that [nature] consisting in being the substratum of the delusion of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is what is intended; for a causality (*upādānatva*) consisting in transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) is untenable in a partless Brahman. Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that Māyā is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) of the phenomenal world, not Brahman. Enough of this digression.

And that non-existence (abhāva) is of four kinds: antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva), absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva), and mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva). Among these, the non-existence of an effect, such as a jar, prior to its production in a cause, such as a lump of clay, is antecedent non-existence. And it is the object of the cognition "it will come to be."

In that very context, the absence of a jar that occurs immediately after the falling of a mallet is *dhvaṃsābhāva* (destructive absence). Even this *dhvaṃsa* is destroyed upon the destruction of its own substratum, namely the potsherd. Nor does this entail the reappearance of the jar, because the *dhvaṃsa* of the jar's *dhvaṃsa* is itself a *dhvaṃsa* whose counter-positive is the jar. Otherwise, if the jar—which consists of the *dhvaṃsa* of its prior absence (*prāgabhāva*)—were destroyed, it would entail the reappearance of the prior absence.

Nor should it be argued that even so, in a case where the locus of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is eternal, how can there be the destruction of that destruction? For if such a locus were distinct from consciousness (*caitanya*), its eternity would be unproven, since it will be stated later that everything other than Brahman is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman. And if the locus of destruction is consciousness itself, then [the reason] is unproven (*asiddhi*), because a destruction whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is superimposed is perceived as being merely the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*). As it has been said:
"For the destruction of an imagined entity is indeed a destruction with a remainder consisting of its substrate."
In this way, the destruction of the silver in the mother-of-pearl is also simply consciousness delimited by "this" (idam).

Absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) is that which does not exist at any of the three times within a given locus; for example, the absolute non-existence of color in air. That [destruction], like space and the other elements, is indeed the counter-positive of annihilation (dhvaṃsa).

Mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is the object of the cognition "this is not that. This very thing is designated as distinction (vibhāga), difference (bheda), and separateness (pṛthaktva), because there is no evidence for a distinction or the like that exists apart from difference. Furthermore, this mutual non-existence is beginningless if its locus is beginningless, as is the case with the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, or the difference between Brahman and the individual soul; it is beginningless even if the locus itself is beginningless. It is, however, beginningless if its locus is finite, such as the difference of a cloth in a jar.

Both types of difference are indeed subject to destruction (*dhvaṃsa-pratiyogin*), because upon the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*), the cessation of those things dependent upon it necessarily follows. Furthermore, difference is of two kinds: qualified (*sopādhika*) and unqualified (*nirupādhika*). Among these, "qualified" means having an existence that is pervaded by the existence of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); "unqualified" means being devoid of that [pervasion].

Among these, the first is as follows: the differentiation of a single space due to the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as a jar; or the differentiation of a single sun due to the difference of vessels of water; or the differentiation of a single Brahman due to the difference of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Differentiation without limiting adjuncts is, for example, the differentiation of a cloth from a jar. Nor is there any contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*) even if one admits the differentiation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) within Brahman; for non-duality remains unimpaired, just as in the case of space and so forth, because no real (*tāttvika*) differentiation is admitted. This is because it is accepted that the phenomenal world is merely superimposed upon the non-dual Brahman. As it was said by Sureśvarācārya:
"What is this intolerance of yours regarding the postulation of its being a means of proof?
Do you not see that the world itself is imagined therein by ignorance?

For this very reason, the qualification "being distinct from antecedent non-existence" in the inference for ignorance in the *Vivaraṇa*, and the qualification "being an entity" in the definition of ignorance in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, are both consistent.

Thus, the cognition of the four kinds of non-existence occurs through the non-apprehension of the capable; therein, non-apprehension is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the aforementioned means of knowledge arises and is known intrinsically (*svataḥ*).

For instance, validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being a cognition that possesses a qualifier in that which possesses it (*tadvati tatprakāraka*), which is common to both memory and experience, and is conducive to successful activity (*saṃvādipravṛttyanukūla*). This [validity] is produced by the general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) of cognition itself; it does not depend on any additional excellence (*guṇa*), because there is no such concomitant excellence in all valid cognitions (*pramā*). Nor is there, in the case of perceptual valid cognition, the contact of the sense organ with many parts [of the object], since that is absent in the perception of color and so forth, as well as in the perception of the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, even when that [contact with many parts] exists, the perception "the conch is yellow" is still an error.

For this very reason, even the consideration of a valid middle term (*salliṅgaparāmarśa*) and so forth is not a "quality" (*guṇa*) in the case of a valid inference (*anumiti*) and other such cognitions; for even in cases involving the consideration of an invalid middle term (*asalliṅgaparāmarśa*), the inference remains a valid cognition (*pramā*) because its object is not sublated. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even an erroneous cognition would become valid due to the lack of distinction in the general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) for cognition; for we accept that the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) is also a cause. Furthermore, this does not entail the doctrine of extrinsic validity (*paratastva*), since extrinsic validity arises only when there is a dependence on adventitious positive causes (*āgantukabhāvakāraṇa*).

And validity is known intrinsically (*svataḥ*). Being graspable intrinsically means being graspable by whatever causal complex grasps its own substratum, provided there is an absence of defects. The substratum is the cognitive modification (*vṛttijñāna*); that which grasps it is the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*). When that cognitive modification is grasped by it, the validity residing therein is also grasped.

Nor does this lead to the impossibility of doubt regarding validity; for in that case, since a defect must also exist in accordance with the doubt, there is no apprehension of validity itself because of the absence of the grasper of its own locus—which is constituted by the absence of defects. Alternatively, *svatastva* (intrinsic nature) consists in the fitness to be grasped by whatever grasper grasps its own locus. Even though the aforementioned fitness exists for validity in a case of doubt, there is no impossibility of doubt, because it is not apprehended due to the influence of a defect.

Invalidity, however, is not produced by the causal complex common to all cognitions, for otherwise invalidity would result even in the case of valid cognition. Rather, it is produced by defects (doṣa). Nor is invalidity apprehended by whatever apprehends its own substratum, because the absence of the object—which constitutes the essence of invalidity—cannot be grasped by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) since it is not presented by a functioning cognition. Instead, it is the object of an inference based on signs such as unsuccessful purposeful activity; thus, invalidity arises and is known only extrinsically (parataḥ). Thus ends the chapter on Non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) in the Vedāntaparibhāṣā. ||6||

Thus, for the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) as defined above, validity is twofold: that which reveals empirical reality (vyāvahārika-tattva) and that which reveals ultimate reality (pāramārthika-tattva). Among these, all means of valid cognition other than those that penetrate the nature of Brahman possess the former kind of validity, because their objects are not sublated during the state of worldly transaction (vyavahāra).

The second [type of scriptural statement], however, consists of those such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1) up to "That thou art" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7), which are intent upon the identity of the individual soul and Brahman; for that identity between the individual soul and the Supreme, which is their subject matter, is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time. And since that identity is known through knowledge dependent upon the knowledge of the meanings of the words *tat* (That) and *tvam* (Thou), the meaning of the word *tat* is first determined by means of its definition and its means of valid cognition.

In this regard, definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is of two kinds: essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and incidental definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*). Among these, that which is the very nature itself as the definition is the essential definition. For example, reality (*satya*) and so forth are the essential definition of Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "He understood bliss to be Brahman. If it is asked, "But how can the nature itself function as a definition, given that a thing cannot reside in itself?"—the answer is: no.

For it is possible for there to be the relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) through the conceptualization of the relation between property and possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) within that very [reality] with respect to itself. As it has been said: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity are properties (*dharma*); although they are not separate from consciousness, they appear as if distinct from it."

An incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) is that which, while not persisting for as long as the object to be defined exists, nevertheless serves to differentiate it. For example, "possessing odor" is the incidental definition of earth, because odor is absent from atoms during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and from jars and other objects at the time of their production. In the present context, however, the definition is "being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world. Here, by the word "world," the entire aggregate of effects is intended; "causality" means agency. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like.

And agency consists in possessing immediate knowledge, desire, and volition directed toward its material cause. Regarding the existence of God’s immediate knowledge of His material cause, the scriptural authority is such passages as: "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge; from Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food. Regarding the existence of His such desire, the scriptural authority is: "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate. And regarding His such volition, there is the statement: "He made that [mind]."

The intended definition consists of three characteristics, each containing one of the factors—knowledge, will, and so forth—as its core; otherwise, there would be the fault of superfluous qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*). For this very reason, only one of birth, maintenance, or destruction is included in the definition. Thus, nine definitions are obtained. And regarding Brahman’s being the cause of the world’s birth and so forth, the scriptural authority is: "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter at their departure," and so on.

Alternatively, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman is its being the material cause (*upādānatva*) of the entire universe. This material causality consists either in being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the world, or in being the substratum for Māyā, which undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of the world. It is with reference to this very kind of material causality that the identity (*tādātmya*) between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is declared in such scriptural passages as: "All this is what this Self is," "It became the existent and the non-existent," and "May I be many, may I procreate.

Even common worldly designations such as "the jar exists," "the jar shines," and "the jar is desired" arise from the superimposition of the identity of the jar upon Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).

If it is objected: "Surely, because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of consciousness whose nature is bliss (*ānanda*), there arises the empirical usage of 'desirability' regarding a jar and so forth; likewise, since suffering (*duḥkha*) is also superimposed there, would there not follow the empirical usage of 'desirability' for that too? We reply: No. For we accept the principle that "when a superimposition occurs, one seeks its cause, but a superimposition does not occur simply because a cause exists. Thus, although the aspect of existence and consciousness (*sac-cid-aṃśa*) may be superimposed upon suffering and the like, the aspect of bliss (*ānandāṃśa*) is not superimposed there. As for the empirical usage of the two aspects of name and form (*nāma-rūpa*) in the world, that is due to the connection with name and form which consist of the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). As it has been said: "Existence, manifestation, and loveliness—these constitute the three aspects [of Being]; name and form are the other two. Thus, there are five aspects."
"The first three are of the nature of Brahman; thereafter, the two are of the nature of the world.

Now, the sequence of the world's birth is described. In that regard, at the time of the initial creation, the Supreme Lord—conjoined with the karma of living beings which is the cause for the diversity of the universe to be created, and accompanied by Māyā characterized by immeasurable and indefinable specific powers—first conceives the entire world consisting of name and form within His intellect and forms the resolve, "I shall do this," according to such scriptural passages as, "It [the Self] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

From that [Unmanifest], the five unevolved elements (apañcīkṛta-bhūta), which are denoted by the term "tanmātra," arise. Among them, sound is the quality of ether (ākāśa); sound and touch are the qualities of air (vāyu); sound, touch, and form are the qualities of fire (tejas); sound, touch, form, and taste are the qualities of water (āpas); and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the qualities of earth (pṛthivī). However, sound is not the exclusive quality of ether alone, because it is perceived in air and the other elements as well. Nor is this a case of error, as there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka) to the contrary.

These elements are composed of the three qualities (guṇas) and are effects of the māyā consisting of the three qualities. The qualities are sattva, rajas, and tamas. From these five elements endowed with the quality of sattva, when taken separately, the five sense organs known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell are produced in their respective order. From these same five elements endowed with the quality of sattva, when combined, the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta) are produced. The presiding deities of the five [organs] beginning with hearing, respectively, are the quarters (Dik), Vāyu, Ārka (the Sun), Varuṇa, and the Aśvins.
The presiding deities of the mind and the other [faculties] are, in order, Candra, Caturmukha, Śaṅkara, and Acyuta.

From these very five elements endowed with the quality of *rajas*, the organs of action—speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—are produced in their respective order. Their presiding deities, in sequence, are Agni, Indra, Upendra, Yama, and Prajāpati. From the five elements combined and endowed with the quality of *rajas*, the five vital airs (*vāyu*) known as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna* are born. Among them, the air that moves forward is *prāṇa*, residing in locations such as the nose; the air that moves downward is *apāna*, residing in locations such as the anus.

The *vyāna* moves everywhere, pervading the entire body. The *udāna* moves upward; it is the vital air of departure and resides in the throat. Through these [subtle elements] endowed with the quality of *tamas* and consisting of unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*) matter, the quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*) elements are produced. This is because the scriptural statement, "And of them, I shall make each one threefold," is intended to indicate the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). The method of quintuplication is as follows: first, dividing ether into two parts, and then dividing one of those parts into four, one combines those four portions with the other elements, such as air and the rest.

Thus, having divided the air (*vāyu*) into two parts and further dividing one of those parts into four, one joins those four portions with ether (*ākāśa*) and the other elements. The same applies to fire (*tejas*) and the rest. In this way, half of each individual element consists of its own portion, while the other half consists of the fourfold [other] elements; thus, the designation of "earth" and so forth among earth and the other elements arises from the predominance of their own respective portions. As it has been said: "But on account of the preponderance [of a particular quality], there is the designation of that [element]; indeed, there is the designation of that."

From those unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūta*), there arises the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), which sustains the journey to the other world, persists until liberation, and is endowed with mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*). It is joined by the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, and the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) beginning with *prāṇa*. As it has been said: "The subtle body, arising from the unquintuplicated elements, is equipped with the five breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the ten organs; it is the instrument for experience."

And that [subtle body] is of two kinds: the higher and the lower. The higher is the subtle body of Hiraṇyagarbha; the lower is the subtle body of those such as ourselves. Among these, the subtle body of Hiraṇyagarbha is called the principle of Mahat (the Great), while the subtle body of those such as ourselves is designated as Ahaṃkāra (the I-maker).

Thus, from the fivefold-compounded elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*) endowed with the quality of darkness (*tamas*), there arises the sevenfold upper worlds known as Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satya; the sevenfold lower worlds known as Atala, Pātāla, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Rasātala, and Mahātala; the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); and the four types of gross bodies known as the viviparous (*jarāyuja*), the oviparous (*aṇḍaja*), the sweat-born (*svedaja*), and the soil-born (*udbhijja*). Among these, the viviparous are bodies born from wombs, such as those of humans, cattle, and so forth.

Egg-born (aṇḍaja) are those born from eggs, such as the bodies of birds, serpents, and so forth. Sweat-born (svedaja) are those born from sweat, such as lice, mosquitoes, and so forth. Sprout-born (udbhijja) are those born by breaking through the earth, such as trees and so forth. Even trees and the like possess the nature of a body, insofar as they serve as the substratum for the experience of the fruits of evil karma.

And here, the Supreme Lord possesses direct agency in the production of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and so forth, in the production of the *liṅga-śarīra* endowed with seventeen components, and in the production of the gross body of Hiraṇyagarbha. Regarding the production of the entire rest of the phenomenal world, he acts through the medium of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, according to the Śruti: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*) and differentiate names and forms.
Hiraṇyagarbha is the first individual soul (*jīva*), distinct from the threefold form [of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva];
as it is said: "He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called the Puruṣa."

"He was the first creator of beings; Brahmā appeared in the beginning," according to such scriptural passages as, "Hiraṇyagarbha appeared in the beginning. Thus has the creation of the elements and their derivatives been described.

Now dissolution (*pralaya*) is defined. Dissolution is the destruction of the three worlds. It is of four kinds: eternal (*nitya*), primordial (*prākṛta*), occasional (*naimittika*), and absolute (*ātyantika*). Among these, eternal dissolution is deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because it consists in the dissolution of all effects. Furthermore, at that time, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) abide in the form of their causes. Consequently, for one who has awakened from sleep, there is no inconsistency regarding pleasure, pain, and so forth, nor is there any inconsistency regarding memory.

Nor is it the case that the activities of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—which depend upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—would be untenable due to the dissolution of that organ during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). For even though, in reality, there is an absence of breathing and such functions, their perception [during sleep] is merely an illusion on the part of other persons, just like the perception of the body of one who is asleep. Furthermore, this does not mean that the sleeping person is indistinguishable from one who is dead; for there is a distinction: the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) of the sleeper remains right here in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), whereas that of the deceased resides in another world.

Alternatively, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) possesses two powers: the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Among these, while the internal organ characterized by the power of cognition perishes during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), that characterized by the power of action does not; thus, the persistence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is not contradictory. Scriptural authority for the aforementioned state of deep sleep is found in such passages as: "When one is asleep and sees no dream, then he becomes one with this prāṇa; then speech, along with all names, merges into him," and "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being (*sat*); he has gone to his own self. These and other such texts serve as proof.

The elemental dissolution (*prākṛtapralaya*), however, is the destruction of all effects caused by the destruction of the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahman*). When, for the effected Brahman who has previously attained the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman, there occurs supreme liberation in the form of disembodied isolation (*videhakaivalya*) upon the completion of his *prārabdha* karma—characterized by his authority over the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—then those inhabitants of that world who have also attained the direct realization of Brahman attain disembodied isolation along with Brahman. As the Śruti declares: "When the time of universal reabsorption arrives at the end of the Supreme, all those of perfected selves enter the supreme state along with Brahman."

Thus, when the Kārya-Brahman is liberated along with its inhabitants, there occurs the dissolution of all the worlds within the cosmic egg presided over by that Brahman, as well as the dissolution of the material elements (bhautika) and beings (bhūta) such as the stationary objects contained therein, into the primordial nature (prakṛti), which is Māyā, and not into Brahman; for destruction in the form of sublation (bādha) resides only in Brahman. Therefore, this is called "prākṛta-laya" (dissolution into primordial nature).

The occasional dissolution (*naimittika-pralaya*) is the dissolution of the three worlds alone, caused by the conclusion of a day of the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahman*). A day of Brahman is measured by a period of one thousand *catur-yugas*, according to the scriptural statement: "One thousand *catur-yugas* are said to be a day of Brahmā. The time of dissolution is measured by the duration of a day, since the duration of the night is equal to that of the day. Regarding both the primordial dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*) and the occasional dissolution, the statements of the Purāṇas serve as authoritative evidence: "When two *parārdhas* of the life of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, have passed, then the seven primordial natures (*prakṛtis*) are indeed prepared for dissolution."

"This is the natural dissolution (prākṛtika-pralaya), O King, wherein [the world] is dissolved"— this statement is the authority for the natural dissolution. "This is declared to be the occasional dissolution (naimittika-pralaya), wherein the Creator of the universe lies eternally upon the seat of Ananta, having absorbed everything into Himself"— this statement is the authority for the occasional dissolution.

The fourth dissolution (*turīya-pralaya*), however, is the liberation of all beings caused by the direct realization of Brahman. In the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), this occurs simultaneously; in the doctrine of multiple souls (*nānājīvavāda*), it occurs sequentially, according to such scriptural texts as, "All become one. Among these, the first three dissolutions are caused by the cessation of karma, whereas the fourth is caused by the arising of knowledge; the distinction is that [in the fourth], it occurs together with the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Thus, the fourfold dissolution has been described. Its sequence is now being determined. The dissolution of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) does not occur according to the sequence of the dissolution of their causes; for at the time of the dissolution of a cause, it is impossible for its effects to remain without a substratum. Rather, it occurs in a sequence inverse to that of creation. This is because, upon the destruction of each respective effect, the destruction of the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) that produced it is the sole operative factor, whereas the destruction of the material cause (*upādāna*) is not the operative factor.

Otherwise, even according to the Nyāya system, it would follow that the color, smell, taste, and other qualities residing in the atoms of earth are not destroyed during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Thus, the dissolution occurs in this manner: earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether (*ākāśa*), ether into the individual ego (*jīvāhaṅkāra*), that into the cosmic ego (*hiraṇyagarbhāhaṅkāra*), and that into primordial ignorance (*avidyā*).
As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O divine sage, the earth, which is the support of the world, dissolves into water."
Water dissolves into fire, and fire dissolves into air.
And the wind dissolves into space, and that [space] dissolves into the unmanifest;
the unmanifest, O Brahmin, dissolves into the partless Puruṣa. Thus it is said.

Being the cause of such dissolution is the *taṭastha-lakṣaṇa* (indirect definition) of Brahman, the referent of that term. Now, one might object: "If Brahman is presented by the Vedāntas as the cause of the world, then Brahman must possess phenomenal manifestation (*saprapañca*); otherwise, the scriptural passages concerning creation would lose their authority. This is not so. For the purpose of the creation passages is not creation itself, but rather non-dual Brahman alone. How, then, is creation useful for the realization of that [Brahman]?

In this way—if the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in Brahman were propounded without first presenting its creation—then, just as color (*rūpa*) negated in air might be suspected of existing elsewhere, there would arise the suspicion that the world negated in Brahman exists elsewhere; thus, non-duality (*advitīyatva*) would not have been established beyond doubt.

Therefore, once the knowledge that Brahman is the material cause arises from the creation passages, any suspicion that the effect might exist elsewhere apart from its material cause is dispelled. Consequently, when its non-existence even in Brahman is established by such statements as "not this, not this," and the world-appearance is understood to be illusory (*tuccha*), Brahman—free from all delusions of duality and consisting of the single essence of indivisible Being-Consciousness-Bliss—is established. Thus, the creation passages have, through this indirect sequence, their ultimate purport (*tātparya*) in Brahman alone, which is non-dual.

The passages concerning the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma*) found in the context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*) have as their sole purpose the superimposition of qualities required by the injunctions for meditation, and not the establishment of those qualities as real. However, the passages concerning the Brahman with attributes found in the context of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) are employed to provide the objects of negation required by the prohibitive statements. Thus, no scriptural passage whatsoever contradicts the realization of the non-dual Brahman.

Thus, some maintain that the denotation of the term *tat* is the Lord-consciousness (*īśvaracaitanya*), characterized by both essential and incidental definitions, which is the reflection of Māyā. Their intention is as follows: the mere consciousness common to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is the original image (*bimba*). The reflection of that very image in Māyā, which consists of nescience (*avidyā*), is the Lord-consciousness; the reflection in the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the individual soul-consciousness. This is according to the Śruti: "This individual soul has the effect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); the Lord has the cause as His limiting adjunct."

According to this view, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is like that between the reflection of the sun in a vessel of water and the sun itself. Because the limiting adjunct consisting of ignorance (avidyā) is all-pervasive, the Lord who possesses that adjunct is also all-pervasive; because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is limited, the individual soul who possesses that adjunct is also limited.

In this view, since the defects produced by ignorance would pertain to the Supreme Lord just as they do to the individual soul (jīva)—because an adjunct (upādhi) invariably favors its own reflection—others hold that the consciousness of the Lord is of the nature of the original object (bimba). Their intention is as follows: there is only one consciousness; when it is characterized by being the original object, it is the consciousness of the Lord (īśvaracaitanya), and when it is characterized by being the reflection, it is the consciousness of the individual soul (jīvacaitanya). Furthermore, regarding the adjunct for the conceptualization of the original object and the reflection: in the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda), it is ignorance (avidyā); in the doctrine of multiple souls (anekajīvavāda), they are simply the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa).

The distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of ignorance and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Furthermore, the defects produced by these adjuncts reside only in the reflection, which is the *jīva*, and not in the original object (*bimba*), the Supreme Lord, because an adjunct "takes the side" of the reflection. In this view, the difference between the *jīva* and the Supreme is like that between the sun in the sky and the reflection of the sun appearing in water or other surfaces. If it is objected: "Since the consciousness of the original object—the Supreme Lord—is absent from the locus of the *jīva* (just as the face situated on the neck is absent from the region of the mirror), He would not be the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all," we reply: No.

When a sky containing clouds is reflected in water or other media, we observe a connection between the reflected image and the entry of the original object—the great sky—into that water; thus, even though a limited original object cannot occupy the same space as its reflection, there is no contradiction in the case of the unlimited Brahman, the original object, occupying the location of its reflection. Nor should it be argued that a reflection of Brahman is impossible because it lacks form, for such reflections are observed only in the case of things possessing form; for even form itself, though formless, is seen to possess a reflection.

Nor is there a rule that a formless substance cannot possess a reflection, for it has already been stated that the Self lacks substantiality (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, the inference of the non-existence of a reflection of Brahman is sublated by such scriptural passages as: "It is seen as one and as many, like the moon in water," and "Just as this luminous self, the sun, though one, enters into many different waters. Thus, the referent of the word *tat* (That) has been defined.

Now the meaning of the term *tvam* (the "thou") is investigated. In the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), the soul is the reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*). In the doctrine of multiple souls (*anekajīvavāda*), however, it is the reflection in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And that [soul] possesses three states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Among these, the state of waking is the state of cognition produced by the senses; there is no over-extension [of the definition] to other states because the senses are absent in those other states. Furthermore, cognition produced by the senses is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ, since the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) is beginningless.

Furthermore, one view holds that this modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) serves the purpose of overcoming the veil (*āvaraṇābhibhava*). To explain: according to the position that the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahitacaitanya*), since the consciousness that is the substrate of objects such as a jar is itself the nature of the individual soul, it would follow that the jar and other objects are always manifest to the soul. Therefore, one must admit the existence of an ignorance that veils the consciousness delimited by the jar and so forth—an ignorance subordinate to the root-ignorance (*mūlavidyā*) which is designated by the term "state" (*avasthā*).

This being the case, there is no consequence of the jar and other objects being manifest at all times, because it is only unobstructed consciousness that serves as the cause of manifestation. Since that obstruction would be eternal, the jar and other objects would never be manifest; therefore, its destruction must be explained. However, mere consciousness is not the generator of that destruction, because that which illuminates the object cannot itself remove its own obscuration.

Nor is it the consciousness conditioned by the mental modification (*vṛtti*), for in that case, [ignorance] would also be removed even in instances of indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*). Therefore, it is said that the mental modification exists for the purpose of subduing the veil, because it either produces the destruction of the veil through a specific modification excluded from indirect knowledge, or because it produces such destruction in the consciousness conditioned by that specific modification.

Another view holds that the function [of cognition] has the purpose of establishing a relation. In that case as well, the individual soul (*jīva*) is undivided, having ignorance (*avidyā*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Although it exists in the location of a jar or other object, it does not manifest the jar and so forth during the state when there is an absence of a direct cognitive function (*aparokṣa-vṛtti*) in the form of the jar, because of the lack of a relation with the jar. However, during the state of a cognitive function in the form of each respective object, it manifests them, because at that time the relation exists.

If it is objected: "Is it not inconsistent to assert the absence of connection for the undivided *jīva*, which—having ignorance (*avidyā*) as its limiting adjunct—is by its very nature connected to all things? Furthermore, if the absence of connection is asserted on the basis of its being 'unattached' (*asaṅga*), then even after the occurrence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), there would still be no connection. To this we reply: We do not deny the general category of connection between the *jīva* and objects such as a jar during the state when a mental modification is absent; rather, what we deny is that specific kind of connection which is the cause for the manifestation (*bhāna*) of the jar.

And that specific relation between the object and the consciousness of the living self (jīvacaitanya), characterized as the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor, is occasional and dependent upon a mental modification (vṛtti) assuming the form of that object. For instance, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), being composed of light (taijasa), is by its very nature capable of manifesting the consciousness of the living self due to its transparent substance; whereas an object such as a jar is not so, because it is not a transparent substance.

However, during the state of conjunction with a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that possesses its own form, the internal organ manifests consciousness immediately after the rise of that modification; for it has the property of having its own inertia (*jāḍya*) overcome by the modification, and it serves as the substratum for the fitness to manifest the consciousness produced by the modification. As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "For the internal organ brings about the fitness for the manifestation of consciousness not only within itself, but also in objects such as jars with which it is in contact. And it is observed that even an opaque substance becomes a receiver of reflections when in contact with a transparent substance."

Just as a wall or similar surface possesses the capacity to receive reflections of the face and so forth during its state of contact with water and the like, and just as a jar or similar object possesses the quality of being a manifestor—which is to say, the quality of receiving those reflections—and just as consciousness possesses the quality of being manifested therein, which is to say, the quality of being reflected there; for the very purpose of establishing such a mode of manifestation, it is accepted that in cases of direct perception (*aparokṣa*), the mental modification (*vṛtti*) goes outside [the body]. However, in cases of indirect perception (*parokṣa*), because there is no contact between the fire and the like and the mental modification, there is no manifestation of consciousness, and thus no directness.

In this view, it should be understood that the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of objects consists in their being manifestors of consciousness (*caitanyābhivyañjakatva*). (The alternative view, however, was stated previously—that the perceptibility of an object such as a jar consists in its non-difference from the knower). Thus, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is unlimited, the purpose of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) has been established as being for the sake of connection [with the object].

Now, the nature of the relationship [between the individual soul and objects] is examined under the view that the soul is limited. For instance, the individual soul (jīva) has the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its limiting adjunct (upādhi). It is not the material cause (upādāna) of objects such as a jar, because it lacks connection with the location of the jar and other such things. Rather, Brahman alone is the material cause of the jar and so forth, because that consciousness conditioned by Māyā (māyopahita-caitanya) pervades all jars and other objects. It is for this very reason that Brahman possesses omniscience.

And so, since it follows that the manifestation of a jar or the like is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) without its non-difference from the Brahman-consciousness which is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that jar, a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the jar is postulated in order to manifest it and to establish that non-difference from the Brahman-consciousness which is the substrate of the jar. Now, one might object: "Even by means of a mental modification, how can the non-difference between the consciousness of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the consciousness of the object be accomplished? For, due to the difference between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the jar and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), non-difference between the two consciousnesses delimited by them is impossible. To this we say: No.

Since it has been stated that there is no difference between the substrata (upadheya) because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its objects reside in the same location—given the acceptance that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) goes outside the body—the application of the *vṛtti* in cases of direct perception (*aparokṣa*) has thus been established according to different philosophical views.

The state of dream (*svapnāvasthā*) is the state of the internal organ’s direct perceptual modification (*aparokṣāntaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) whose object is not produced by the sense organs (*indriyājanya*). The term "not produced by the sense organs" is used to exclude the waking state (*jāgradavasthā*). The term "internal organ" is used to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which possesses modifications of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*).

Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is a state of the modification of ignorance (*avidyā-vṛtti*), which falls within the domain of ignorance. Since the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) during the states of waking and dreaming are themselves forms of ignorance, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to those two states. Regarding this, some maintain that death and fainting constitute distinct states, while others hold that they are included within deep sleep itself. As for whether these two are included within or excluded from the three states, since they are of no utility in defining the meaning of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*), we shall not exert ourselves to resolve them here.

Its unity is in relation to the adjunct of *māyā*, while its plurality is conventionally designated in relation to the adjuncts of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). By this, the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is refuted; for in such passages as, "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the Self, the lower [Self] is seen to be even as small as the tip of an awl," the atomicity of the *jīva*—which is conditioned by the dimension of the internal organ denoted by the word "intellect"—is heard. Furthermore, that *jīva* is self-luminous with respect to the state of dream, according to the scriptural text: "In this state, this person is self-luminous."

And [the Self] is of the nature of experience, according to such scriptural texts as, "He is indeed a mass of pure consciousness. The conventional usage "I experience," however, is justified by taking into account the consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*). Thus, the meaning of the term *tvam* (Thou) has been defined.
Now, the identity of the meanings of the terms *tat* (That) and *tvam* (Thou), which is the subject matter of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), is being stated. [Objection:

But is this not contradicted by perception such as "I am not the Lord," by the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the substratum of contradictory attributes such as limited knowledge and omniscience, and by such scriptural texts as, "Two birds... and, "There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable..."?
All beings are the perishable; the unchanging is called the imperishable.

If it is argued that, since the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*) is understood through such Smṛti passages, statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) must have only a figurative meaning—just like sentences such as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*) or "The grass-bundle is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*)—we say: no. This is because perceptual cognition of difference, which may involve defects in its instruments, is sublated by the knowledge produced by the Veda, whose defects are impossible. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that the science of astronomy, which apprehends the moon's vast dimensions, would be sublated by the perception that apprehends the moon as being merely the size of a thumb.

Furthermore, according to the maxim "when a jar is red after baking, [one says] 'this is red, not black,'" perception apprehending the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) has as its object the difference between the attributes that serve as qualifiers; for this reason, inference (*anumāna*) is also not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it contradicts scripture (*āgama*), just like the inference that Mount Meru is composed of stone.

Nor is there any contradiction with other scriptural passages; for between a statement that is primarily intended to convey a certain meaning and one that is not, the former is more authoritative. Thus, compared to passages such as "Two birds... which merely restate a difference established in the world, the statements such as "That thou art" are more powerful, as they possess a specific intention toward non-duality determined by their opening and concluding sections and other internal indicators.

Nor is there any impossibility of the individual self (*jīva*) and the Supreme Being (*para*) being one and the same on the grounds of their being substrata of contradictory attributes. For just as cold water can appear to be the locus of heat due to an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), so too it is possible for that which is by nature devoid of qualities to appear as the locus of agency and other such states due to adventitious conditions such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And if heat is merely superimposed (*āropita*) upon water and the like, then the same applies to the present case as well. Nor should it be argued that, since according to our system (*siddhānta*) agency is non-existent anywhere at all, how can there be a superimposition in the absence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior cognition of the object to be superimposed; for [the process of superimposition] proceeds from the beginningless cycle of transmigratory existence.

Because, for the sake of parsimony, its causality is established solely by its being a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the object of superimposition. Nor is there any difficulty regarding the initial superimposition, since the stream of superimpositions such as agency (*kartṛtva*) is beginningless. Furthermore, although the two qualified referents denoted by the words *tat* and *tvam* are unfit for identity, the identity of their respective indicated essences (*lakṣyasvarūpa*) has indeed been established. For this very reason, sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), which convey that [identity], possess the nature of imparting an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*), just like the sentence "This is that" (*so 'yam*).

Furthermore, validity does not belong exclusively to those [cognitions] directed toward an action (*kārya*), because in cases such as "Caitra, a son has been born to you," the apprehension of the relationship between word and meaning occurs even with respect to an already established fact (*siddha*). Thus, it is established that the subject matter of the Vedānta scripture is the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self (*jīvaparaikya*), which is not contradicted by any means of valid knowledge and is propounded by the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas. This concludes the section on the determination of the subject matter.

Now, the purpose (*prayojana*) is being defined. That which, once known, is desired as residing in oneself is the purpose. It is of two kinds: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*). Among these, pleasure (*sukha*) and the absence of pain (*duḥkhābhāva*) are the primary purposes. The means to either of those is the secondary purpose. Pleasure is also twofold: with gradation (*sātiśaya*) and without gradation (*niratiśaya*). Therein, pleasure with gradation is a specific manifestation of a fragment of bliss produced by the varying degrees of mental modifications (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) arising from attachment to sense objects.
For the Śruti declares: "Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very bliss.

Furthermore, Brahman alone is unsurpassed happiness, according to such scriptural passages as, "He understood that bliss is Brahman," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss. Liberation is the attainment of Brahman, whose nature is bliss, and the cessation of sorrow; for the Śruti says, "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. Liberation is not the attainment of another world, nor is it the sensory happiness produced therein; for since such things are created, they would be impermanent, which would entail the possibility of the liberated soul returning once again.

If it is objected: "In your view as well, if the attainment of bliss and the cessation of evil were beginningless, the same defect would apply; if they were beginningless, then activity toward hearing [the scriptures] and so forth for the sake of liberation would be untenable"—we reply: No. For liberation, which is already established as the very nature of Brahman, activity toward its means is justified by the delusion that it is unestablished. Furthermore, the cessation of evil is also already established as being the very nature of Brahman, which serves as its substratum. Even in the world, it is observed that the attainment of what has already been attained and the avoidance of what has already been avoided constitute valid purposes.

Just as when gold or the like has been forgotten though held in one's hand, one obtains what was as good as unobtained through the instruction of a trustworthy person that "the gold is in your hand"; or just as for a man who mistakes a garland wound around his foot for a snake, the avoidance of the very snake already avoided is well known upon hearing the words of a trustworthy person that "this is not a snake"—in the same way, there is the attainment of bliss even though it was already attained, just as the avoidance of a snake is well known even though it had already been avoided.

Thus, liberation (mokṣa) has as its purpose the attainment of the bliss already attained and the cessation of the misfortune already eliminated. And that [liberation] is to be accomplished solely through knowledge. This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey," and because there is an invariable rule that the cessation of ignorance is to be accomplished solely through knowledge.

And that knowledge has as its object the identity of Brahman and the Self, according to the Śruti: "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness; then you knew yourself alone, [realizing] 'I am Brahman'," and according to the statement of Nārada: "The knowledge arising from sentences such as 'That thou art' is the means to liberation. Furthermore, that knowledge is of the nature of direct perception (aparokṣa), because if it were indirect (parokṣa), it would be impossible for it to remove an error that is itself direct.

Regarding that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), some hold that it arises from such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*); others maintain that it arises solely from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) when refined by reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*). In this regard, the intention of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*) is as follows: it has been established that the immediacy of consciousness (*saṃvid*) is not dependent upon the production of a specific instrument (*karaṇa*), but rather depends upon the specific nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Consequently, since Brahman is non-different from the cognizing individual soul (*pramātṛ-jīva*), the knowledge produced by words directed toward It is also immediate.

For this very reason, in the *Pratardana-adhikaraṇa*, regarding the statement spoken by Indra to Pratardana—"I am Prāṇa, the conscious self; meditate upon me as life and immortality"—once it has been determined that the word *prāṇa* refers to Brahman, a doubt is raised concerning the apparent inconsistency of the use of the first-person pronoun "me" (*mām*) in the phrase "meditate upon me. As a response to this, the Sūtra states: "But the instruction is by means of scriptural vision, as in the case of Vāmadeva. Here, the term "scriptural vision" (*śāstradṛṣṭi*) is explained as "vision based on scripture," referring to the realization "I am Brahman" produced by statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
Thus, it is this knowledge that is denoted by the word "scriptural vision."

However, their intention is as follows: the perceptuality of cognitions is based solely on the specific nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*), not on the specific nature of the object (*viṣaya*), because we observe the practical distinction between perceptuality and non-perceptuality regarding the very same subtle object depending on whether the instrument is sharp or dull. Thus, since being produced by a sense organ (*indriyajanyatva*) alone is the determinant for the directness of consciousness, a cognition produced by words does not possess immediacy (*aparokṣatva*).

Even in the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), the mind alone—refined by reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—is the instrument, according to such scriptural passages as, "It is to be perceived by the mind alone. Furthermore, the scriptural texts stating that Brahman is inaccessible to the mind refer to the unrefined mind. Nor does this entail the impossibility of Brahman being known through the Upaniṣads; for the mind as we have described it functions only after the knowledge produced by the Veda, and thus depends upon the Veda. This is because accessibility through other means of knowledge that do not depend on the Veda is precisely what constitutes a contradiction to being accessible through the Veda.
The *Śāstradṛṣṭisūtra* is also consistent with the view that mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) concerning Brahman is produced by the scripture (*śāstra*). As it has been said:

"Even in the case of intense contemplation (*saṃrādhana*), the valid cognition born from meditation on the meaning of the scripture is considered 'vision through scripture' (*śāstradṛṣṭi*); indeed, Vācaspati alone knows it thoroughly."

And that knowledge arises from the destruction of evil, which in turn results from the performance of ritual action; thus, there is an indirect application of ritual actions [to the attainment of liberation]. For this very reason, scriptural passages such as, "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," and traditional texts (smṛti) such as, "When the impurity has been cooked away by ritual actions, then knowledge arises," are both harmonized.

In this way, hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are also means for knowledge; for in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, after restating the vision [of the Self] in the words "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," there is the injunction of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption as its means in the words "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon. Hearing is a mental activity conducive to determining the purport of the Vedāntas regarding non-dual Brahman.

Reflection (*manana*) is a mental activity that produces knowledge in the form of reasoning conducive to dispelling doubts regarding contradictions with other means of valid cognition concerning an object already ascertained through verbal testimony. Meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) is a mental activity conducive to the steadiness of the mind upon the Self, having withdrawn the mind—which is being dragged toward sense objects by beginningless, difficult-to-eradicate latent impressions—from those very objects.
