In this context, *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is the direct cause for the immediate realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as: "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the power of the Divine Self, hidden by its own qualities. Furthermore, *manana* (reflection) is the cause for *nididhyāsana*, because for one who has not performed reflection, there is an absence of firm conviction regarding the subject matter, and thus *nididhyāsana* directed toward that object would be impossible.

Furthermore, hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the cause of reflection (*manana*); for in the absence of hearing, there can be no reflection conducive to determining what is appropriate or inappropriate regarding the subject matter of what was heard, since there would be no verbal cognition due to the lack of certainty concerning the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Some teachers have declared that all three of these are causes for the arising of knowledge.

Others, however, maintain that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is primary, while reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), although subsequent to hearing, are auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it because they bring about the vision of Brahman—which is the fruit of hearing—by way of being remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*). Yet even this status as an auxiliary is not of the nature of a "subordinate element" (*śeṣatva*) according to the third book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]; for such a subordinate relationship must be established by one of the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and in the present case, its occurrence is impossible due to the absence of any such means of proof like *śruti*.

For instance, unlike the cases of "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) or "one offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), there is no scriptural mention of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) to establish that reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Nor is there any indicative mark (*liṅga*)—such as the capacity of mantras like "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) to manifest the act of cutting the sacrificial grass—to be found here. Furthermore, there is no sentence enjoining reflection and meditative concentration by restating the hearing [of the scripture], such as the sentence "he performs the *pravargya* rite at the *agniṣṭoma*" which enjoins the *pravargya* mentioned in another location.

Nor is there, within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—which are understood from the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" to be the means to that fruit—the mention of hearing (śravaṇa), just as there is the mention of the Prayāja offerings and so forth within that same context; for hearing is not understood here as being a means to the fruit in the same way those [offerings] are.

If it is argued that—since hearing (*śravaṇa*) is enjoined by restating the act of seeing in the phrase "it is to be seen," and since hearing possesses a fruit, the acts of reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), which are mentioned in proximity to it within the context of hearing, must be subordinate to it by virtue of that very context according to the logic of the *prayāja* offerings—[we reply: no. For in another scriptural passage such as "They, following the yoga of meditation, beheld," meditation is understood to be the means for attaining vision; thus, when that meditation requires subordinate elements, reflection and hearing themselves would result in being subordinate to it by the same logic of the *prayāja* offerings.

Furthermore, the sequential order (*krama*) and the name (*samākhyā*) have already been refuted at length. Moreover, the inquiry into whether the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are auxiliary (*aṅga*) is purposeful: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *prayāja*s would not be performed in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*s), whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), they are performed there as well. In the present case, however, hearing (*śravaṇa*) is not the archetype (*prakṛti*) of anything, such that reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) might also be performed there as a result of the inquiry into their status as auxiliaries. Therefore, reflection and meditative concentration do not possess the status of being auxiliaries in the sense of the third book (*Tārtīya*).

However, just as in the case of an effect such as a jar, where the lump of clay and so forth are the primary causes (*pradhāna-kāraṇa*) and the wheel and so forth are the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), leading to the designations of "primary" and "secondary," so too should it be understood regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). This has been indicated by the teacher Vivaraṇācārya: "The ascertainment of the word, qualified by its power and intended meaning, is the cause for the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) without any intervention, because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-intervening with respect to the comprehension of its object."

"But reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), by means of their effect—which is the one-pointed mental modification (*ekāgra-vṛtti*) perfected through the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the mind’s inclination toward the inner self—attain the status of being causes for the experience of Brahman. Thus, reflection and meditative contemplation, which are the remote causes with respect to the fruit [of liberation], are accepted as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) to the ascertainment of the word qualified by its purport (*tātparya*), which is the immediate cause."

And seekers of liberation possess the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and the other [means of knowledge], because one who desires a fruit is qualified for optional (kāmya) ritual action, whereas for the desire for liberation, there is the application of the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, and tranquility (śama), self-control (dama), withdrawal (uparati), endurance (titikṣā), concentration (samādhāna), and faith (śraddhā). Tranquility is the restraint of the internal organs; self-control is the subduing of the external organs; withdrawal is the absence of distraction; endurance is the capacity to endure the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat; and concentration is one-pointedness of mind.

Faith (*śraddhā*) is confidence in the words of the Guru and the Vedānta. Here, by the word "withdrawal" (*uparama*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is intended; thus, some maintain that only renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) have the qualification for hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*). Others, however, argue that since the word "withdrawal" does not denote renunciation, and since the mere absence of distraction is possible even for householders—as evidenced by the fact that Janaka and others are heard to have engaged in the inquiry into Brahman—the injunction for hearing and so forth applies equally to all stages of life (*āśrama*). Even meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*) is a cause for the direct realization of the undifferentiated Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahma-sākṣātkāra*) by means of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*). As it has been said:
Those who are dull-witted and unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman devoid of distinctions are shown compassion through descriptions of Brahman with attributes.
"When their minds have been brought under control through the practice of the Brahman with attributes (saguṇabrahma),
that very [Brahman] shall manifest directly, free from the conceptualization of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Thus, for those who meditate upon the Brahman with attributes and, having gone to the world of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi-mārga), have produced the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra) right there, liberation occurs together with Brahman.

For those who possess karma and have gone to the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) by way of the path of smoke, when their karma is exhausted through experience, they are reborn among beings from Brahmā down to stationary objects (*sthāvara*), in accordance with their previously performed good and evil deeds. Thus says the Śruti: "Those of pleasant conduct enter a pleasant womb; those of foul conduct enter a foul womb. As for those who practice what is forbidden, having experienced intense suffering accumulated by their respective sins in specific hells such as Raurava, they are reborn among animal species such as pigs, or among stationary objects and so forth. Enough of this elaboration arising from the context.

However, for one who has attained the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahman*), there is no departure to another world, according to the scriptural text: "His vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart. Rather, having experienced pleasure and pain until the exhaustion of his *prārabdha* karma, he is subsequently liberated. If it is objected: "Since the destruction of all karma by knowledge is established through such scriptural texts as 'And his actions perish when He, the higher and the lower, is seen,' and through the traditional text (smṛti) 'The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes,' the persistence of *prārabdha* karma is untenable"—we reply: No.

This is because, according to such scriptural passages as "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united," and such traditional texts as "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish," it is understood that only accumulated (*sañcita*) karmas—distinct from those karmas that have already produced their effects—are destroyed by knowledge.
Accumulated karma is of two kinds: good (*sukṛta*) and evil (*duṣkṛta*). Thus says the Śruti: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds."

If it is objected: "But surely, when the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is removed by the knowledge of Brahman, its effects—the *prārabdha* karma—would also be removed; how then is the maintenance of the body for the knower (*jñānin*) possible? We reply: No. For it is only unobstructed knowledge that removes ignorance; we do not admit the removal of ignorance during the state of obstruction caused by *prārabdha* karma. If it is further objected: "Even so, upon the liberation of one person through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there would be the liberation of all, because ignorance (*avidyā*) is one; once it is removed, transmigration (*saṃsāra*) could not exist anywhere," We reply: No. Some say this is acceptable, as it is a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Others, however, in order to avoid this very defect, say that one must accept a plurality of ignorances (*avidyā*) supported by the plural Vedic scripture, "Indra [acts] through illusions" (*indro māyābhiḥ*).

Still others maintain that there is only one ignorance, but that the powers of that very same ignorance to veil the nature of Brahman are manifold according to the distinction between individual souls (*jīva*). Thus, since they accept that for one who attains knowledge of Brahman, there is the destruction of the ignorance characterized by the power to veil the nature of Brahman, but not the destruction of the ignorance characterized by the power to veil the nature of Brahman with respect to others, it does not follow that when one is liberated, all are liberated.

For this very reason, in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office" (3.3.32), a doubt was raised regarding the impossibility of the continued bodily existence of authorized persons (*adhikāri-puruṣas*) such as Indra and others, even though they have attained knowledge of reality; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was that liberation without a body (*videha-kaivalya*) occurs immediately after the completion of the *prārabdha* karma that necessitated their office. As stated by the teacher Vācaspati Miśra: "Those who, having completed their office as impelled by the Lord—who is gratified by the perfection of their meditations and other practices—enter the supreme state."

Furthermore, this [doctrine] is not tenable under the view that the liberation of one entails the liberation of all. Therefore, even under the theory of a single ignorance (*avidyā*), the systematic arrangement [of individual experiences] must be established by admitting a distinction in the veils (*āvaraṇa*) for each individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, it is established that the purpose [of the inquiry] is liberation through the knowledge of Brahman; and that liberation consists in the cessation of evil and the attainment of unsurpassed Brahman-bliss.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Vedāntaparibhāṣā* composed by Śrī Dharmarāja Dīkṣita.
